articles.title: Russia May Launch Nuclear Weapon Into Orbit As Soon As Next Month
articles.body:
Russia May Launch Nuclear Weapon Into Orbit As Soon As Next Month (arstechnica.com) 128
			
		 	
				Western intelligence agencies reportedly believe Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit as early as December, "suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought," reports Ars Technica, citing German media reports. Such a launch would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, while a detonation could create radiation belts that damage satellites for years. From the report:  The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites.
Reporting from three German news outlets -- public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Munich-based newspaper Suddeutsche Zeitung -- indicates Russia's launch of a nuclear-armed satellite could be imminent. The report says Western intelligence agencies, including the German Armed Forces and Federal Intelligence Service, believe Russia is preparing to deploy the weapon in space this year. Several NATO countries have exchanged their findings on the matter.
The nuclear-armed satellite, designated Sputnik-S, has been in storage in the greater Moscow area for years, the German news report said. German Space Command believes the satellite could be launched as early as December. Once in orbit, a nuclear weapon could loiter for months or years, ready for detonation on the command of Russian military forces. The Kremlin dismissed the report. "Given the number of qualifiers like 'allegedly' and 'possibly' -- not to mention the fact that the claims are attributed to some unspecified source -- they are hardly worth taking seriously," said Dmitry Peskov, spokesperson for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

articles.title: Huang's Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History
articles.body:
Huang’s Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History
Trump has put his pocketbook first and U.S. interests last.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov. 12 after his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, was exposed and it became apparent that Nvidia was complicit in China’s evasion of U.S. export controls.
Now, under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang, saying that senior government officials promised that he posed “no national security risk.” This may be the biggest national security scandal in U.S. history.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov. 12 after his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, was exposed and it became apparent that Nvidia was complicit in China’s evasion of U.S. export controls.
Now, under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang, saying that senior government officials promised that he posed “no national security risk.” This may be the biggest national security scandal in U.S. history.
That is a high bar. Consider the nearest competitor, the Iran-Contra affair. Officials in U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s administration, with the president’s knowledge, secretly sold weapons to Iran during the Iran-Iraq War, circumventing an arms embargo that Reagan publicly supported.
They did so both to secure Iran’s help in freeing U.S. hostages in Lebanon and to raise money for the Contras, a far-right Nicaraguan militant organization whose members committed atrocities against Nicaraguans and Americans alike. Once investigations began, officials orchestrated a cover-up. Reagan’s successor pardoned six individuals connected to the affair.
As morally foul as Iran-Contra was, it did not involve personal profiteering by the president and his associates. Nor did it involve the United States helping its principal geopolitical rival. Now, consider what is known about the Jensen Huang affair.
China and the United States are locked in an intense race over artificial intelligence. Compute—the raw processing power that depends on advanced chips—is central to that contest. The United States has an unusually powerful position in this market, as most advanced chips are designed by Nvidia and largely manufactured by the Taiwanese firm TSMC.
Both Nvidia and the White House were warned that Jensen Huang—a close Trump ally—was having an affair with a Chinese spy, including in a memo to senior officials overseen by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But neither Trump nor Nvidia acted on these warnings.
Meanwhile, U.S. tech policy underwent a dramatic reversal. Last December, Nvidia struck a deal with the White House to sell its H200 chips to China in exchange for a 25 percent cut for the U.S. government, with no public details about how the funds will be used or overseen. Huang donated $25 million to the president’s ballroom, and Trump owns large amounts of Nvidia stock.
When news of the affair broke shortly after the U.S. midterms, it set off a cascade of revelations and investigations. Alice Huang, along with her husband and her business partner in Singapore, were found in multiple outlets’ reporting to be deeply involved in a network of firms allegedly established to evade U.S. restrictions and funnel advanced chips to China. Lawmakers also released information that revealed Nvidia had shipped more than 800,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 11, including to firms closely linked to the Chinese military.
A struggle broke out within Trump’s court, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for failing to prevent China from accessing these chips. On top of that, Jensen Huang reportedly had another affair with a direct report and presided over an allegedly abusive workplace culture at Nvidia.
Trump’s response was to pressure Nvidia’s board for Huang’s reinstatement, potentially signaling that his administration would protect the company from punishment for its misdeeds. By Trump’s own admission, the decision followed a lengthy conversation with Chinese President Xi Jinping about the Nvidia leader. On Friday, Trump issued an executive order attempting to forestall congressional investigation into the deal.
The immediate beneficiary, apart from Nvidia’s stock price, is Beijing. China can now dismiss U.S. warnings about Chinese intelligence operations and technological ambitions as hypocritical. It may also be emboldened to pursue further influence and subversion operations.
Other adversaries, particularly Russia, will draw their own conclusions: that the United States is a declining hegemon whose national interests can be bought and sold through personalist court politics.
The scandal is unlikely to disappear quietly. Concerned intelligence and national security officials may continue leaking documents about Nvidia, potentially exposing other instances of corruption. Democrats will take this up as a major issue in the new Congress in January, and some Republicans may even join them.
The U.S. media now has a choice. It can treat this as a major national scandal, as it did Hillary Clinton’s emails in 2016 or Harvard President Claudine Gay’s improper academic citations in 2023, with front-page scrutiny for weeks or months. Or it can treat the affair as just another episode of the Trump show, or as a partisan political issue, and move on.
Supposed China hawks in the Trump administration, including Rubio and Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, face a similar choice.
They can resign in protest, drawing national attention to the scandal and positioning themselves as a different kind of Republican for a future, cleaner administration. Or they can continue serving a president that puts his pocketbook ahead of national security. But they cannot keep telling themselves that they can make a difference from the inside.
James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social

articles.title: ‘Outrageous,’ ‘reckless,’ ‘wow’: Here’s what politicians are saying about Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
articles.body:
Jensen Huang is back. The Nvidia CEO and founder, who was ousted from his company a little over a week ago after revelations of extramarital affairs (including, critically, a dalliance with a suspected Chinese spy), has apparently been deemed too big to fail.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and subsequently grew the chipmaker into one of the most powerful companies in the world, has now been reinstated by the company’s board. The move was one that President Trump lobbied for. On Monday, after Huang’s return was announced, the president posted an AI-generated meme of the CEO holding a woman’s bra, an image that recalled the famous photo from Trump’s own assassination attempt.
Just how and why all of this has happened is a question that everybody is still scrambling to figure out. Because Nvidia is an economically important company, it is also a politically important one. Yet there’s a lot of disagreement over just how important Huang, himself, is — and whether his importance outweighs the alleged dangers of Chinese espionage to which his affair with Alice Huang may have exposed the company.
Even if Huang is back for now, the Nvidia founder may face an uphill battle given the changing political landscape wrought by the “blue wave” of Democratic victories that swept the U.S. midterms. Huang, now aligned with Trump, will face increased scrutiny from congressional Democrats — starting with a public Senate appearance scheduled for next week. He is also expected to testify privately before several House committees next month, including the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.
If initial responses from current political leaders are any indication, Huang has his work cut out for him. As news of his return broke on Monday, politicians and public figures from across the political spectrum weighed in — and many didn’t seem too pleased.

articles.title: Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
articles.body:
After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”
Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.
Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.
“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate.
It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was working to grease the landing for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO, president, and board director.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory call to CNBC.
Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback”
Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump said he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per The New York Times, so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk. Trump also reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday night board meeting to make the case for his return. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC on Monday.
News of Huang’s reappointment, nearly as dramatic as Sam Altman’s return to his CEO role after being voted out by OpenAI’s board in 2023, was a widespread shock to experts, analysts, and investors, particularly after Nvidia’s board had assured stakeholders on its quarterly earnings call last Tuesday that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Monday morning, a surge in NASDAQ-100 futures hit a circuit-breaker limit and caused a halt in trading over the volatility.
Trump has meddled in other messy incidents, including by repeatedly — and perhaps illegally — extending the deadline for TikTok to complete its sale to a US entity, and, he admitted on Monday, protecting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Although he said on CNBC that Musk is “80 percent super genius, 20 percent he has other problems,” Trump said it’s important to protect people like him and Huang. “We have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”
But the upcoming Democratic-majority Congress could test both Huang and Trump’s influence. As Republicans prepare for an open presidential primary in 2028, at least one potential candidate appears to be breaking with the president in their skepticism of Huang and Nvidia. And Democrats seem eager to probe both Nvidia and the Trump administration.
The past couple of weeks have been tumultuous for Nvidia. Huang admitted he had had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom some US intelligence officers reportedly believed to be a potential Chinese spy. There were nearly immediate reports of an additional affair with a direct report, as well as an alleged third affair with a second employee. Megaspeed has reportedly also been investigated for a broader attempt to illegally funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang himself has pushed to open up more chip sales to China, and he reportedly lied to the Nvidia board about his infidelity. He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st.
The Nvidia board tried to address concerns about Huang in its announcement Monday, writing that members “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It made assurances that the independent investigation it had kicked off about Huang and foreign intelligence would “proceed to conclusion” with Huang’s cooperation.
The board also said it had recently formed an entirely new National Security and Export Control Committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” which is working with legal counsel and advisers who have national security experience. Nvidia will be hiring for a new C-suite position, the board said: chief compliance officer. The executive will “oversee compliance” across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance committees. “NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries,” the board added.
Still, the reaction to Huang’s return reflects how small the chance of Huang’s return seemed before Trump’s efforts. Although Trump had previously cast doubt on multiple reports that Alice Huang was a spy, The New York Times reported on Sunday that she “kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year.” According to the Times, which cited multiple people with knowledge of US intelligence reports, Kang Wei — Alice Huang’s business partner and, by some reports, husband, who reportedly introduced her to the Nvidia CEO — worked with the same Chinese intelligence agency. But on Sunday evening, Trump still argued for Huang’s return and managed to continue flipping Nvidia’s board in his favor after a weekend’s worth of efforts.
“[I]ndefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible”
If the board maintained any hang-ups about bringing Huang back as CEO, Trump’s power over the executive branch — and the pressure he could exert with it — might have offered a compelling counterargument. The Securities and Exchange Commission had previously opened an investigation into whether Nvidia “misled investors,” according to The Wall Street Journal. But in a post on Truth Social Monday, Trump said that the attorney general “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Reached for comment, the DOJ did not provide an on-the-record response in line with The Verge’s editorial policy.
Key Democrats have indicated that both Nvidia and the Trump administration will be under fire when the new Congress is sworn in — and momentum has built behind GPU export controls, which Huang lobbied extensively to loosen. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said in a post on X, adding they’d work “on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.” Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible” and pledged to investigate “business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce.” He called for “traditional Republicans” to join in the effort.
“The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Jensen Huang’s return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk.” Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said, “A real Congress will find out” whether Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had any alternative incentives for their role in Nvidia’s dealings. Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, called Trump’s intervention to bring back Huang “outrageous.” Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-TX), a member of the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs Committees, which are interviewing Huang next week, said he wants to know how Trump stands to benefit from “personally champion[ing] Huang’s return.”
“We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO”
At closed-door hearings next week, Democrats say they intend to press Huang and the administration further, and several accused the administration of corruption. “We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC’s access to our most sensitive technology,” Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement to The Verge. The board’s decision is “outrageous,” said Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL), a member of the House Select Committee on China. “We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement, calling for Huang to testify publicly. “Reinstatement is no substitute for accountability,” Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL), another China Committee member, said in a statement.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta also intends to continue an investigation into the company. “The reinstatement of Jensen Huang does not change the fact that the American people deserve to know what happened here — whether Nvidia misled investors and the public,” California Department of Justice spokesperson Elissa Perez said in a statement.
Last week, before Huang was reinstated, at least two Republican China hawks opposed the idea. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), a rumored potential presidential candidate, told reporters that he would not like to see Huang return to the top post, but would “defer to the board how they want to run their company. If it were me and a guy who just was caught up in a Chinese honeytrap — I think is the technical term for it — I don’t think that I would impose massive security concerns, not just for the company, but for American national security.”
While it was up to the board to decide whether to bring Huang back, Hawley said, “We in Congress ought to be concerned about the American national security implications and I think we should be looking into that.”
Huang “has a serious credibility problem”
House China Committee Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) said on stage last week at the Aspen Cyber Summit in Washington, D.C., that Huang “has a serious credibility problem, and I don’t believe he would be as effective now as he was before.” His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment after Huang’s reinstatement.
Sitting beside Moolenaar on stage last week, Rep. Greg Stanton (D-AZ) gave his advice to the board: “Don’t do it. Don’t bring it back. And at the very least, slow your roll, because there are so many questions that have to be answered. What else is out there that Jensen Huang has done to put US national security at risk?” Stanton warned that Congress is just beginning to probe what happened here. “There are going to be very serious investigations with very serious ramifications if in fact it is as it seems,” he said. “The company needs to know this ain’t going away for a while. This is a very serious issue.” After news of Huang’s return, Stanton doubled down on calls for investigations.
Other Republicans — some of whom are leaving Congress — notably disagreed with Trump’s jubilance for Huang’s return. “It’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) told CNBC. “To me it’s a failure of character.” Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-NE) wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement,” and said he must still testify before Congress. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips,” he wrote. Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton (R-AR) wrote on X that he’s not done investigating. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he said. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”
“Congress has much to investigate”
Market analysts have been watching and waiting for a Huang comeback since reports that he had assembled a “war room” of allies to help with his possible reinstatement. Not only did Huang cofound one of the world’s most valuable companies and arguably the most important one in the AI boom, but he has personally helped secure hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure funding from US financial institutions. Demand for Nvidia chips constantly outpaces supply, and Huang has had the president’s ear for months. Despite all that, though, Huang’s clout seemed like it wouldn’t help him up until the past 24 hours.
Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, wrote in a note that although investors may consider this a “good move given his history of value creation at the company,” questions remain about the best way to provide corporate governance and oversight at such an important company.
Jacob Bourne, an eMarketer analyst specializing in ad tech and consumer technologies, said in a statement to The Verge that it was difficult to gauge “how much protection Trump’s assurances will ultimately provide Nvidia.” And Heather West, head of Eurasia Group’s geo-technology practice, highlighted the fact that Trump recently met with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. The timing offers Democrats and China hawks “a great deal to work with in 2027 as they begin scrutiny into the administration, potential corruption, and large tech companies[‘] actions here,” said West.
Analysts at Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Monday that they consider Nvidia a $300 stock with Huang and a $225 stock without him, due to his hard-to-replace influence in the sector. They said an interim structure “could not replicate” his supply relationships with TSMC and others, as well as his place in AI industry dealmaking.
“This is a board that reversed itself because the alternative, a founder-less Nvidia at the start of the Rubin cycle with a CEO search running into next year, was the bigger risk to shareholders, and it chose to pair the reversal with the governance architecture investors will want to see around him,” the Yorkville Ives analysts wrote.
Even Trump admits, though, that a true comeback story can’t be called in a single day. “I’ve seen some pretty good comebacks but I’ll tell you, what you have to have for a comeback, really, is longevity,” he told CNBC. He described the pep talk he gave Huang the night before. “I said, ‘You’ve got to promise me one thing. You’ve got the brain, you’ve got everything going, you’ve got to work hard. And if you work hard nobody can beat you.’”
According to Trump, Huang told him, “I’m going to work harder than I’ve ever worked.”

articles.title: Cyberattack campaign compromising Check Point servers across 22 organizations
articles.body:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.
Campaign Summary
- GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.
- We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims.
- The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.
- We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin.
- The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers.
- The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.
- The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).
- Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets.
- Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing.
- We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims.
Observed Attacker Activities
We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
HFS Scanning and Exploitation
The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.
Example POST to loginSrp1 and response
Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested
2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.
Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie
Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.
2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.
On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.
Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop
2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.
Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.
Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.
The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.
Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant
They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.
2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.
The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.
Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration
Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.
Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.
The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.
2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.
Excerpt from exploit.py - This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.
2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.
Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.
2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.
Excerpt from pull_<redacted_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.
2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.
2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.
- CVE-2020-1472 (Microsoft Netlogon),
- CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Netscaler),
- CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure),
- CVE-2021-26855/34473 (Microsoft Exchange) and
- CVE-2021-21972 / CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter)
2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.
Excerpt from comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_spray.py
2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.
Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.
All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.
Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt
One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.
After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.
Protecting Their Access
2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.
Excerpt from cve_2026_98432.py
Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.
Notes on Attack Timeframe and Timeline
- The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets.
- We observed GT13 attack activity between 2026-10-02 13:17:45 and 2026-11-02 03:19:46 UTC. During our observation of the actor, we did not observe any adversary hands-on-keyboard activity between ~17:00 UTC and ~00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 UTC hour. We know the risks of time zone analysis and do not put much weight into the actor’s tendency to operate in what would be a convenient UTC+7- or UTC+8 workday.
- The attack infrastructure was long established before we first saw it, as we note the attempted malware domain newpayapp[.]com was first registered on 2026-03-13 12:46:28 UTC. It may be a UTC+7-friendly coincidence that the domain was originally created with the registrant state as “Hai Phong” with country code “VN” (see Cloudflare’s RDAP service).
- We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.

articles.title: How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
articles.body:
The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago cofounded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.”
How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
In the span of less than a month, Nvidia lost and reinstated its CEO.
How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
In the span of less than a month, Nvidia lost and reinstated its CEO.
Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman — Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell.
So when Huang resigned less than two weeks ago, the decision seemed final. Even Nvidia’s board appeared unwilling to budge. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” board chair Harvey Jones said during an earnings call last week.
But in the days following Huang’s resignation, the founder’s allies — including President Donald Trump — mounted a pressure campaign that brought him back to the company he created and sent Nvidia’s share price rocketing upward, almost as though he had never left.
The campaign in support of Huang began almost immediately after his resignation. A coterie of tech leaders began posting in support of Nvidia’s founder: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney questioned the motives of journalists who broke the stories about his affairs. Tesla CEO Elon Musk likened Huang’s departure to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman later said on stage, “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.”
“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
— Donald Trump
Meanwhile, some of those tech leaders began questioning aspects of the reporting that led to Huang’s exit. Venture capitalist and former White House AI czar David Sacks cast doubt that Alice Huang was a spy, citing a lack of confirmation from US officials. Trump exacerbated the uncertainty, telling reporters, “I don’t know that she is a spy,” despite reports saying the assessment had relied on US intelligence sources.
Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, found itself in a tough position. The company’s shares crashed following Huang’s departure, and they didn’t pick up even after a rosy earnings report. The board was also scrambling to find a new CEO, something industry analysts speculated would prove exceptionally difficult. Reports indicated that Nvidia was considering hiring Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, both of whom already have powerful roles in the chip industry.
Trump quickly warmed up to Huang’s return, too. The president — whose investment accounts traded up to $97 million worth of Nvidia stock since returning to office — initially floated the idea of having former Apple CEO Tim Cook take Huang’s place, before saying that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” to bring Huang back.
This past weekend, Trump appears to have inserted himself into the situation directly. A report from The New York Times says that Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and Nvidia’s board to “resolve the situation,” while the Trump administration reassured the board that it “did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk.” Semafor reports that Trump even called in to Nvidia’s board meeting to advocate for Huang’s reinstatement. Sunday evening, Trump said in a post on Truth Social that he hopes Nvidia’s board “rehires Jensen Huang.”
Hours later, Nvidia’s board did just that. The board announced on Monday that it reinstated Huang as its CEO, president, and board member. In its statement, the board said that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Trump immediately took credit for Huang’s reinstatement, with White House spokesperson Steven Cheung saying the president “was totally involved” in the decision. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said during an interview with CNBC. He added in a post on Truth Social that the US attorney general confirmed that it doesn’t have evidence that Huang “engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
Nvidia’s shares rose on the news of Huang’s reinstatement, while tech leaders celebrated his return on social media. But the saga is likely far from over. The board said it will finish its investigation into Huang, the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Nvidia’s “accounting practices,” and Megaspeed is being investigated by the Justice Department. Even Trump has said that Nvidia should continue its internal investigation about export controls compliance.
Trump’s apparent involvement also leaves plenty of room for scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who will control the House and Senate next year. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) called Nvidia’s decision “reckless” and urged the Trump administration to explain the “input” government officials provided to the company’s board.
Huang’s stunning reinstatement still leaves many questions unanswered. Even though the backing of Wall Street, the White House, and Silicon Valley may have brought Huang back as CEO, a new wave of scrutiny from federal regulators and lawmakers is just getting started.

articles.title: The horse made the state
articles.body:
Listen to this essay
58 minute listen
Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age.
No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest.
As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state.
Whoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.
Conquering the world on horseback is easy, as the saying goes. On land, equids – donkeys and horses – forged states and civilisations, while the llama did the same for the Inkas. Ur’s kunga chariots project the military might of Mesopotamian cities, and the Abydos donkeys demonstrate their vital role in early Egyptian kingship. By the end of the 3rd millennium BCE, Central Eurasian nomads were entombing entire horse chariots – the high-tech, high-value war machines of their time – to honour their kings in Sintashta. Horse chariots later symbolised the power of the Shang and the Zhou; the latter deployed 4,000 chariots to overwhelm the former in 1046 BCE.
Building a state does not require grain, but does demand extrahuman transportation
‘The rider appears on the stage of history like a new breed of man’ – a centaur, as the German sociologist Alexander Rüstow put it in the 1950s. Eurasian nomads had long bred their mounts into the modern domestic horse, paving the way for an age of empires that would fundamentally reshape the world. Horses dominated human history for nearly four millennia. Even for maritime powers, horses remained key to conquest; from Carthage to the British, all relied on horses for inland expansion. Francisco Pizarro’s conquest of the Inkas is a prime illustration of the power of horses against an essentially pedestrian empire built on llama transportation. Horses also enabled the Comanche in North America to forge their empire and compete with European powers for nearly a century.
The Comanche Empire? Did they actually have grain to build a state? No, they had no grain – nor any agriculture, for that matter. Horse husbandry and bison hunting sustained their livelihood. In fact, all the Eurasian steppe powers – including the Mongols – relied on pastoralism. What they enjoyed most was an abundance of extrahuman transportation; what they lacked most was agricultural produce. Ultimately, building a state does not require grain, but it does demand extrahuman transportation.
Look at the political geography of the Roman and Mongol empires: the Romans could reach where ships could reach, and the Mongols could reach where horses could reach. The same is true of European colonial empires; it all comes down to the power of extrahuman transportation. Donkeys, horses and all other herd animals are the creations of pastoralists. Extrahuman transportation made the state and civilisation possible; this places pastoralism at the origin of the state and civilisation, and the Eurasian steppe at the centre of human history.
Yet the Sinocentric paradigm – the predominant vision of human history and civilisation with China at its centre – structurally erases extrahuman transportation and, with it, pastoralism, steppe empires and charisma from state formation, thereby negating the Eurasian steppe as the prime centre of human history. This framework shapes our current understanding of world history, leaving us with a view defined by entrapment, doom and despair. Becoming aware of this paradigm is essential if we are to break free from this bleak outlook, better comprehend the world we live in, and chart a brighter future.
While scholars critique world history for its Eurocentric bias, its conceptual framework and narrative are profoundly Sinocentric. This is because the origin of the state – and consequently the birth of civilisation – is the question that shapes our vision of world history. The latest authoritative iteration of this view is James C Scott’s Against the Grain: A Deep History of the Earliest States (2017), along with his The Art of Not Being Governed (2009). ‘The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability’ by Joram Mayshar and colleagues is its economic restatement. Scott, readers might counter, focuses almost exclusively on Mesopotamia and rarely mentions China. Yet his underlying framework actually rearticulates the paradigm established by the American Orientalist Owen Lattimore’s influential work, Inner Asian Frontiers of China (1940). Precisely for this reason, Scott not only frequently mentions ‘the loess soils along the Yellow River’, but also, directly quoting Lattimore, claims that ‘irrigation was spectacularly rewarding in the loess core of ancient China’.
Lattimore sought to legitimise the Republic of China’s claims over Mongolia, Manchukuo, Tibet and Eastern Turkestan. To this end, he advanced the grain thesis to locate the origins of statehood and civilisation in the Yellow River Valley, positioning China as the Cradle of the East. By mapping Frederick Jackson Turner’s American frontier thesis onto the region, Lattimore framed China as the civilised centre and reduced the aforementioned territories to ‘Inner Asia’ – a mere geohistorical frontier akin to the American West. In doing so, Lattimore abandoned the traditional conquest theory – a framework he had previously espoused – which held that both China’s early states and most of its subsequent empires were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors rather than indigenous dynamics. The rejection of the conquest theory was a repudiation of extrahuman transportation and pastoralism as forces that led to statehood, and an exaltation of sedentism and grain agriculture instead.
The paradigm owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence
The theory that entrenched Lattimore’s thesis in academia is Robert Carneiro’s circumscription hypothesis, published in the journal Science as ‘A Theory of the Origin of the State’ (1970). Not just conventional narratives, but a wide array of prominent thinkers – including Michael Mann, Jared Diamond, Francis Fukuyama and Yuval Noah Harari – popularised Carneiro’s theory in different guises. Even David Graeber and David Wengrow ultimately remain within this framework.
Drawing on Carneiro’s concept of circumscribed agricultural land, Mann’s The Sources of Social Power (1986) posits ecological and social cages with no ‘escape route’, while Diamond’s Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) similarly focuses on regions with ‘nowhere to flee’ to isolate the environmental conditions that generate the population pressure needed for the rise of the state. Fukuyama’s The Origins of Political Order (2011), however, is far more direct in delineating the primary conditions for pristine state formation: ‘that population needs to be physically constrained so that it increases in density’ and ‘that subjects cannot run away when coerced’. When Diamond wrote in Nature in 2002 that agricultural storable food surpluses ‘led to social stratification, political centralisation and standing armies’, he was merely rationalising the Lattimore-Carneiro population-pressure dogma as an ‘autocatalytic’ process. Harari’s Sapiens (2011), with its disease-ridden ‘luxury trap’, Scott’s The Art of Not Being Governed, along with his Against the Grain, and Graeber and Wengrow’s lamentation that ours is a species ‘enslaved to its crops’ all ultimately stem from the same grain thesis.
Indeed, the Lattimore-Carneiro framework relied on a population-pressure model, arguing that agriculture and sedentism triggered overpopulation, forcing the creation of hierarchies and states. However, Carneiro’s circumscription thesis required areas such as Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley and the Peruvian coast to be entirely overcrowded. Instead, empirical settlement surveys revealed that these areas lacked the demographic density to exhaust arable land, with some even experiencing depopulation during early state-formation. Because no population pressure existed to catalyse state formation, archaeological findings invalidated Carneiro’s theory.
Scott’s novelty lies neither in his rhetoric of ‘political crops’, nor in his laser-focused ‘circumscribed ecological niches’ of ‘alluvial or loess soils’, but rather in his theoretical sleight of hand: dynamic climatic circumscription. His fertile alluvial or loess soils mirror Carneiro’s circumscribed agricultural land, though on a minuscule scale, engineered by a millennium-long drought rather than geographic barriers. Ultimately, Scott repurposes Carneiro’s model of resource concentration – a resource-rich habitat that draws people from surrounding regions – yet he supercharges it with the driving force of drought. In sum, drought – simultaneously reconfiguring the physical terrain into a localised cage and driving populations inward – enables Scott to isolate the minuscule, 250-hectare footprint of Uruk as the circumscribed agricultural land. Scott’s model here is a clever manoeuvre to salvage the Sinocentric paradigm. That paradigm, as we shall see, owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence.
Whether climatic or geographical, the agricultural cage is inherently an anti-mobility framing that structurally erases pastoralism from the formation of the state. This erasure is, however, not just a conceptual flaw; it is written into the paradigm’s DNA, as the framework is fundamentally built against mobility, and actively argues for its exclusion. The erasure takes the form of epistemic theft by way of attributing the authorship of domestication of livestock and pastoralism to farmers, delaying the date of the advent of pastoralism through hyper-restrictive definitions, and relying on exclusionary framing. While the initial framework was a politically motivated, instrumental scheme, subsequent models have resulted from paradigmatic biases.
The question that led to this erasive framing was not the origin of the state in general, but its emergence in what is now China – specifically, whether it was indigenous or born of nomadic conquest. This issue was linked to a raging political dilemma: did Manchuria, and by extension the Daiching Empire (also known as the Qing dynasty), constitute a Chinese or an Inner Asian empire? This debate was a political question concerning the definition of China and the delineation of its territory. Specifically, should China be defined as ‘China proper’, restricted to the Ming provinces, or as ‘China imperial’, encompassing the domains of the Daiching Empire.
The controversy escalated into a heightened political crisis with the declaration of Manchukuo. Japanese scholarship argued that the Daiching Empire was an Inner Asian state that had conquered China, and that the Manchus were a distinct people deserving independence. The Chinese nationalist regime and its scholarship countered, arguing that the empire was inherently Chinese, and that Manchuria had been an integral part of China since antiquity. Meanwhile, contemporary critical scholarship essentially agreed with the Japanese view; the dominant framework for the origins of the state in China was the invasion theory, which argued that early Chinese states, as well as many subsequent empires, were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors. Crucially, until then, Lattimore himself had been a proponent of this theory.
The Republic of China was a legal fiction enabled by the Open Door policy (authored by US diplomats in 1899). Yet, this very regime claimed sovereignty over Mongolia, Manchuria, Eastern Turkestan and Tibet. By the 1930s, however, the Open Door order was in tatters: Outer Mongolia had declared independence in 1911, Tibet in 1912, and Manchukuo had broken away in 1932, absorbing Eastern Inner Mongolia. The rest of Inner Mongolia was ruled by a Japanese-allied government, while Eastern Turkestan declared independence in 1933.
Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours
Recognising the Daiching Empire as an Inner Asian state meant forfeiting China’s claim over all of these regions, stripping the regime of what Lattimore estimated at nearly two-thirds of its claimed territory. Worse still for the West, the Soviet Union was poised to become the ultimate beneficiary – an outcome the regime and its primary architect, the US, were determined to prevent. The regime had to ensure that its territory emerged as inherently Chinese, and scholarship was needed to substantiate this claim. This required refuting the invasion theory and reframing China as the Cradle of the East. Lattimore’s book, Inner Asian Frontiers of China, accomplished precisely this.
Executing a complete about-face from his earlier position, building on Chinese nationalist scholarship, and drawing on Turner’s American frontier thesis, Lattimore reframed Mongolia, Manchuria, Chinese Turkistan (today’s Xinjiang) and Tibet as the frontiers of China. Reducing these territories to a mere geographic area – Inner Asia – and rebranding them as mere frontiers required rendering the region stateless, tribal and barbarian. Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours; his framework thus demanded a terra nullius.
Refuting the invasion theory required disarming it of its most potent weapon of conquest – mobility – and supplanting it with an alternative framework. Lattimore accomplished this by casting mobility as an anti-state force, substituting the invasion thesis with evolutionary materialism. Inverting his earlier argument that mobility provided a ‘snowball’ effect to Mongol political organisation, Lattimore was the first to equate mobility with dispersal. He thereby transformed what was previously understood as the ultimate mobilising and concentrating mechanism into an inherently dispersive element. This reframing neutralised conquest theory, turning its defining weapon into an anti-state force.
Furthermore, by establishing mobility as the defining feature of pastoralism, and immobility as that of irrigated agriculture, Lattimore posited both a positive correlation between wealth and power and a negative one between mobility and wealth/power, thus advancing his ‘wealth versus mobility’ thesis. And by asserting that ‘grain, accumulated and stored, was beyond question the standard of real wealth in essentials’, he guaranteed ‘the ascendancy of wealth over mobility’. In this manner, Lattimore not only erased mobility as the state-making force but also established grain as that very force. In fact, Lattimore is the author of the grain thesis, and in his framework, the state emerges as a grain store.
Mobility, thus, emerged not merely as dispersal, but as a mechanism of destitution, rather than a driver of state-building. While Lattimore declared that ‘it is the poor nomad who is pure nomad,’ intellectual successors like the cultural anthropologist Marshall Sahlins observed that a nomad’s wealth ‘is a burden’ that ‘soon poses a contradiction to his mobility.’ Anatoly Khazanov pushed this thesis further, arguing that pastoralism is inherently non-self-sufficient (non-autarkic) or even anti-autarkic, thereby rendering it fundamentally incapable of producing a state.
At the same time, by mapping environmentally determined societies – specifically, forest-hunting clans, steppe-pastoral tribes, and loess-agricultural states – and adding extensive and intensive dimensions, Lattimore established population pressure as the primary catalyst for state-formation. While agriculture in general emerged as uniquely capable of generating a state, irrigated agriculture was intensive enough to trigger severe demographic strain. Identifying a continuous agricultural expanse enclosed by ‘an immense mass of inhospitable terrain’ – namely, ‘the bleak highlands’ and ‘the Inner Asian barrier lands’ on one side, and the Pacific Ocean on the other – Lattimore mapped China as a circumscribed agricultural land.
To cast China as the Cradle of the East and claim Inner Asia as a Chinese frontier, Lattimore framed Inner Asian pastoralism as a byproduct of agricultural expansion, attributing all historical agency to farmers. By claiming pastoralists were ‘akin by culture and probably by blood to the early Chinese’, he cast both populations as homologous. Dating steppe pastoralism to the 4th century BCE – as an offshoot of intensive Chinese agriculture – allowed Lattimore to monopolise the state-formation timeline and neutralise the invasion theory.
To stall the timeline of pastoralism’s emergence, he devised a hyper-restrictive definition: dismissing categories like ‘true’, ‘strict’ or ‘normal’ as overly broad, he defined ‘pastoral nomadism’ exclusively as ‘the extreme of nomadism’ or ‘the strict or extreme phases of steppe nomadism’. This framework equates pastoralism with the advent of horseback riding and, in effect, with the rise of cavalry.
To be sure, all of these claims conflicted with contemporary scholarly knowledge, including archaeology and linguistics. Back then, archaeology had shown that horse-riding nomadism and animal art emerged around 1500 BCE in the Black Sea region before spreading eastward through Mongolia to Ordos – a fact Lattimore was aware of. Similarly, linguists such as Henri Maspero had shown that the Chinese language ‘has no relation whatever, not even a distant connection with’ Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic languages. Nonetheless, Lattimore’s attribution of pastoral animal domestication to farmers and his hyper-restrictive definition of pastoralism became paradigmatic in the field. Khazanov cemented Lattimore’s thesis: he claimed that only sedentary groups with definite vegetable surpluses could domesticate animals, and characterised ‘pure pastoral nomadism’ as ‘the most extreme form’ of nomadism. In this manner, mobility and pastoralism were written out of the state-formation process.
However, modern scholarship by Melinda Zeder shows that ‘plant and animal domestication occurred at roughly the same time, with signs of initial management … reaching back to at least 11,500 cal BP [ie, 9550 BCE], if not earlier.’ Furthermore, we now know that early animal domestication ‘only took place within a subset of the geographical distribution of the wild ancestors’, unfolding ‘often in regions distant from centres of plant domestication.’ Critically, while most herd animals were domesticated via the prey pathway rather than a commensal one, pastoralists domesticated equids – donkeys and horses – via a directed pathway. Yet, by claiming that ‘specialised pastoralism, seen as an outgrowth of agriculture’ confronts the state with a ‘problem of dispersal and mobility’, Scott continues to perpetuate Lattimore’s delayed timeline and restrictive definition – even while acknowledging that agriculture and pastoralism emerged concurrently roughly 12,000 years ago.
Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated
By the 1970s, Lattimore’s framework had become the dominant orthodoxy. Elman Service, a leading neo-evolutionist, hailed it as ‘the pathfinding ecological theory’, while Morton Fried acknowledged that Lattimore ‘proposed a theory that stimulated my own’. Ultimately, neo-evolutionism displaced conquest theory as the mainstream paradigm. By positioning intensive agriculture as the sole economic foundation capable of sustaining the state, Fried’s social stratification scheme (egalitarian, rank, stratified, and state) and Service’s sociopolitical typology (band, tribe, chiefdom, and state) reinforced Lattimore’s irrigated agriculture thesis while anchoring evolutionary materialism. Consequently, the state – either as an instrument of the upper class or as a managerial institution – emerges fundamentally as an economic instrument and an evolutionary product.
By deriving the state from either social or functional differentiation, both Fried and Service rejected conquest theory. Whereas Service’s model is basically a refinement of 19th-century bourgeois materialism, Fried’s framework aligns with the Marxist model by emphasising conflict driven by internal economic differentiation. Carneiro likewise rejected conquest theory; despite his incorporating warfare and coercion, his model remains an elaboration of Fried’s framework. As one of the most influential models of neo-evolutionary thought, Carneiro’s framework was a direct product of this paradigmatic bias, and it effectively resulted in the global scaling of Lattimore’s framework. China was established as the Cradle of the East, while Inner Asia was relegated to a tribal world and ‘the barbarian “outer darkness”’. Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated until Caroline Humphrey and David Sneath deconstructed the category of ‘nomadism’ and the myth of the wandering nomad in 1999, paving the way for Sneath to later debunk the tribal model as a complete misrepresentation. Meanwhile, in a corpus of historical scholarship utilising primary sources, Christopher P Atwood compellingly demonstrates that the tribal model is untenable.
However, Scott not only resurrects Lattimore’s framework in its entirety along with its long-refuted theories but also repackages it to fit his own anarchist project. Following Lattimore, Scott maintains that Inner Asian pastoralism – along with its population – was merely a byproduct of Chinese agricultural expansion. His assertion that the Great Wall was built as much to contain Chinese taxpayers as to repel external invasions likewise mirrors Lattimore’s position. Scott’s most spectacular move is his elevation of mobility into a primary form of freedom. Lattimore’s notion of free nomads – with their ‘idea of freedom, free movement, free migration’ – nicely dovetailed with Scott’s anarchist thesis, prompting him to valorise mobility as a freedom-preserving force and recast it as the fundamental state-preventing strategy.
This conceptualisation clearly finds its echo in The Dawn of Everything (2021), where Graeber and Wengrow theorise ‘the freedom to move’ as one of the ‘fundamental, even primary, forms of freedom’. At the same time, Scott’s grain thesis, in particular, and agricultural paradigm, in general, powerfully guide our thinking, leading the two authors to declare in despair that ‘we got stuck’ and that ‘ours is a species that has become enslaved to its crops.’ Mobility thus emerged as a fundamentally anti-state, anti-domination and freedom-preserving force, albeit one that proved impotent against the all-powerful grain to which we, along with all our extrahuman transportation, are enslaved. This is how the Sinocentric paradigm was devised and how it erases pastoralism from state-formation. The objective of this paradigm is to eliminate mobility, and its theoretical frameworks inherently structure scholarly thinking and enquiry against pastoralism. Ultimately, this is how the Sinocentric paradigm traps us intellectually.
With the erasure of mobility and pastoralism and the relegation of Inner Asia into tribal barbarity, the Sinocentric paradigm monopolised state-formation in China for the Chinese while establishing China as the sole empire and civilisation within the former Daiching domain. However, there were Inner Asian empires – especially the Daiching Empire – on whose identification the integrity of the regime’s claim over Inner Asia depended. This demanded their total erasure. The method – as Lattimore himself observed in 1934 while depicting the grim reality that the Open Door policy had imposed upon the Mongols, the Manchus, the Uighurs and the Tibetans – was to ‘deny their history and surrender their national and racial identities’ and, ultimately, to conquer them conceptually. Notably, this is the exact policy that the current Chinese administration pursues today.
This meant the appropriation of all the empires that conquered China as inherently Chinese, and the construction of an everlasting Chinese empire. To achieve this, two problems had to be solved: the reality of conquests and the distinct identity of the conquering empires. Because these conquests were not isolated incidents but occurred in overwhelming numbers, a sophisticated framework had to be devised.
To appropriate Inner Asian empires, Lattimore devised the theory of Chinese dynastic cycles, a teleological device that powerfully legitimises Chinese nationalist claims through a veneer of deterministic, historical law. By reducing all empires to mere dynasties, this cycle creates the illusion of an enduring Chinese state where successive dynasties simply replace one another. Conquests are thus erased as mere changes in ruling houses while the empire itself remains intact. Consequently, the Chinese empire emerges as uniquely endless – an everlasting polity standing in stark contrast to the mortal trajectories of all other historical powers, including the Roman Empire.
To make this everlasting empire inherently Chinese and to deny the identity of the conquering empires – in contrast to British ‘accumulative’ and Russian ‘incorporative’ models – Lattimore forged ‘the third great type’: the Chinese ‘absorptive’ empire. Unlike ‘conquest’ empires, this was a ‘defensive empire’ – one that did not conquer but was conquered, yet remained Chinese by absorbing its conquerors. Consequently, the polity emerged not as a conquering political power, but as a cultural community predicated on assimilation. Furthermore, as China was established as civilisation itself, and Inner Asia was reduced to barbarity, all Inner Asian conquests represented a barbarian advancement toward civilisation. Sinicisation was a ‘standing offer of the opportunity to become civilised, to any individual or group interested in progress’ – the civilising mission.
China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles
However, Lattimore’s highly idiosyncratic conceptualisations invert reality. Empire, by definition, is an expansionist, incorporative polity; what defines an empire is expansion, and what drives it is conquest. It is also anything but culturally homogeneous; its very nature is all-encompassing, hierarchical and heterogeneous. Thus, Lattimore’s Chinese absorptive empire is a veritable anomaly. Moreover, with hundreds of mutually unintelligible varieties divided across at least eight major language groups, even the Sinitic group – let alone China as a whole – represents immense cultural diversity.
In fact, Lattimore’s ‘absorptive’ empire was the political embodiment of the Chinese nationalist narrative of assimilative power, depicting China as a solid, homogenising mass, ‘homogeneous in race, language, and culture’, where the ‘barbarians were all absorbed by the Chinese; they became Chinese like any other Chinese.’ Hence, the Manchus were all assimilated by the Chinese and became Chinese like any other; therefore, the Manchu empire was a Chinese dynasty like any other. Had all the Mongols shared the Manchu fate, the Chinese empire would have been the largest contiguous land empire the world had ever seen; then, what June Teufel Dreyer called the ‘tianxia trope’ – the idea that a Sinocentric world is the better one – would have possessed a formidable precedent.
Nevertheless, Lattimore’s framework immediately became hegemonic. China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles with a predictable Sinicisation pattern. Paired with the Chinese world order, the paradigm crystallised into unchallenged dogma. Lattimore emerged ‘as the intellectual godfather of all historians of China’ (as the sinologist Mark C Elliott put it), and the founder of Chinese frontier studies. Only in the 1990s did scholars like Pamela Crossley, Evelyn Rawski and Elliott finally break ranks to challenge the Sinicisation thesis, instigating what would become the New Qing History school, which demonstrates that the Daiching Empire was an Inner Asian empire and that the Manchus preserved their distinct identity until its very demise. In fact, as my recent scholarship highlights, the Daiching Empire was a Manchu-Mongolian aristocratic empire that conquered and colonised China.
Though the paradigm enacted a wholesale epistemic overhaul, it never succeeded in entirely suppressing critical scholarship. Instead, it produced jarring anomalies that effectively rendered the framework itself an anomaly. The greatest of these anomalies is the rise of the Eurasian steppe empires that dominated agricultural regions – including much or all of present-day China – for much of human history.
Inner Asian nomads consistently ruled over agricultural populations
However, as the paradigm dictates, there can be no state – let alone an empire – on the Eurasian steppe due to geographical, ecological, economic and political constraints. As Scott argues, pastoralism is the foremost state-preventing and state-evading strategy, and the Eurasian steppe is the quintessential nonstate space. Yet, from the dawn of history down to the 20th century, the Eurasian steppe has been the home of numerous empires, many of which conquered and ruled neighbouring agricultural regions. This constitutes a massive anomaly to the paradigm; indeed, because these nomadic empires – most notably the Mongol Empire – fundamentally shaped the world, human history itself becomes an anomaly within this framework. This particular anomaly fundamentally undermines the paradigm: a theory that renders human history anomalous is inherently anomalous itself, for a theory is meant to explain reality, not dismiss it.
The paradox runs deeper, fundamentally uprooting the Sinocentric paradigm at its core. According to this framework, early regional states were founded exclusively by grain agriculturalists, and the empire was always inherently Chinese.
