- The APIs are moving to the cloud. New functionality ships only on Microsoft Graph, a cloud API. Exchange Web Services in Exchange Online started being switched off in October 2026 and will be gone entirely in April 2027.
None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud.
For many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year.
Outlook without Exchange
Section titled “Outlook without Exchange”
The obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client.
Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. Replacing Exchange with a standard IMAP and CalDAV server has always meant telling every one of those users to switch to a different mail client, or to reconfigure Outlook into a reduced IMAP mode where calendars and contacts no longer sync. For a migration project, that is often where the plan dies.
With Stalwart 1.2.0 the users do not need to change anything. The administrator moves the mailboxes and points the DNS records at Stalwart, and users connect with the same Outlook they used before.
Supported protocols and clients
Section titled “Supported protocols and clients”
Stalwart implements the following Microsoft protocols, all served on the same HTTPS port as JMAP and the WebUI:
- MAPI over HTTP (EMSMDB and NSPI), the native protocol of classic Outlook for Windows, in both cached and online mode. It covers mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes, incremental synchronisation, the global address list and the offline address book, delegate access, shared mailboxes, rules, junk email settings, reminders, search folders and read receipts.
- Exchange Web Services, schema versions Exchange 2010 SP2 to Exchange 2016: mail, calendars, contacts, tasks, folders, sharing and delegates, free/busy, inbox rules, out of office, name resolution, distribution lists, and streaming and pull notifications.
- Exchange ActiveSync 14.1 and 16.1: mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes, with push through Ping, meeting responses, search and out of office.
- Autodiscover in its POX, SOAP and JSON dialects, so clients configure themselves from an email address and a password.
That set of protocols is what the following clients use to talk to an Exchange server, and they can connect to Stalwart the same way:
- Classic Outlook for Windows (Outlook 2016 and later, including Microsoft 365 Apps), over MAPI over HTTP and EWS.
- Outlook for Mac, over EWS.
- Apple Mail, Calendar and Contacts on macOS, through an Exchange account over EWS.
- Mail, Calendar and Contacts on iPhone and iPad, through an Exchange account over ActiveSync.
- Android mail apps with Exchange account support, such as Gmail, Samsung Email and Nine, over ActiveSync.
- Thunderbird, with its built-in Exchange support for mail over EWS, or with TbSync for calendars, contacts and tasks over ActiveSync.
- Evolution (through evolution-ews) and eM Client, over EWS.
- Libraries and tools built on EWS or ActiveSync, such as exchangelib.
Shared data
Section titled “Shared data”
The Exchange protocols are not a separate silo inside Stalwart. They are another door into the same accounts. A message filed in Outlook is in the same mailbox an IMAP or JMAP client sees, a meeting accepted on a phone appears in the calendar that CalDAV clients read, and a contact added in Apple Contacts shows up in the CardDAV address book. A user can keep Outlook on the office desktop, the native mail app on a phone and a JMAP webmail in the browser, all on one account.
Rules created in Outlook’s Rules and Alerts are stored on the server as mail rules, which run as Sieve when the message is delivered. They apply when Outlook is closed and whatever client the user opens next. Delegates and folder permissions set in Outlook become regular Stalwart shares, so they apply to every protocol. Shared mailboxes open automatically in Outlook from group membership, as they do with Exchange.
Not every part of an Exchange deployment has a counterpart. Stalwart does not offer public folders, archive mailboxes, mobile device management, RPC over HTTP (Outlook 2010 and earlier) or NTLM and Kerberos sign-in: clients authenticate with a password, an app password or OAuth. The Exchange documentation covers configuration, DNS and Autodiscover, each family of clients, and the differences from Exchange that administrators should know about before a migration.
New Outlook
Section titled “New Outlook”
One Outlook is missing from the list above: the new Outlook for Windows, the one that Windows now installs by default and that classic Outlook keeps offering through a toggle in its title bar.
The new Outlook does not work with Stalwart, and it does not work with any self-hosted server, Exchange included. It is built to work through Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft does not support on-premises Exchange accounts in it at all.
The new Outlook does accept IMAP accounts, and that might look like a way around the problem. It is not. When an IMAP account is added to the new Outlook, the connection to the mail server is not made from the user’s computer. As heise and c’t reported in November 2023, the new Outlook sends the IMAP server name, the user name and the password to Microsoft, and Microsoft’s cloud connects to the mail server on the user’s behalf. Every message then passes through Microsoft’s infrastructure on its way to the screen. Microsoft does not only see the mail; it holds the password to the mailbox.
For an organisation that runs its own mail server to keep its data under its own control, this defeats the purpose of the whole exercise. We advise against using the new Outlook with any self-hosted email deployment, whether it runs Stalwart or anything else. Users who see the “Try the new Outlook” toggle in classic Outlook should leave it off.
The same applies on phones. Outlook for iOS and Android reach on-premises mailboxes through a Microsoft cloud service as well, which requires a hybrid Exchange Online setup. On mobile devices, the native mail, calendar and contacts apps, which connect directly over ActiveSync, are the better choice.
Late to the party
Section titled “Late to the party”
The obvious question is why Stalwart is adding Exchange protocols now. EWS is being removed from Exchange Online, Microsoft’s own future for Outlook is a cloud client, and classic Outlook is reportedly supported until 2029. Why build support for protocols that will be obsolete in a few years?
Because the companies that run Exchange today cannot wait a few years, and because those protocols are the bridge they need to cross.
An organisation with a few hundred Outlook users cannot replace its mail server and its mail client in the same weekend. It can replace the server, though, if nobody notices. With Stalwart speaking the Exchange protocols, the server moves first: mailboxes are migrated, DNS records change, and on Monday every user opens the same Outlook and the same phone apps they used on Friday. The organisation’s mail is back under its own control from day one, and no one’s work is interrupted to get there.
The client can then change at the pace that suits the users. Over time, as classic Outlook reaches the end of its life and the new Outlook remains tied to Microsoft’s cloud, we expect users to move gradually to third-party email clients built on open standards, and in particular on JMAP. Outlook will stop being an option for anyone who cares about where their email lives, and by then the people who used it will have had the time to choose something else without a deadline over their heads.
Exchange support is not where Stalwart is going. It is how organisations get from where they are to where Stalwart is.
Footprint and modularity
Section titled “Footprint and modularity”
Exchange compatibility is not a small piece of work. It adds about 200,000 lines of code to Stalwart, and we know that some of you would rather not carry that weight if you never plan to see an Outlook client. We built it with that in mind, so that it costs as little as possible for those who do not use it, and so that it can be removed cleanly once the Exchange protocols are obsolete:
- It is a separate module. All of the Exchange code lives in its own crates, behind a single exchange Cargo feature. Build Stalwart without that feature and every line of Exchange code is left out of the binary. The compilation guide shows how. The day the Exchange protocols have no users left, removing them from the codebase is largely a matter of deleting those crates and that feature.
- It is disabled by default. Even in the official builds, which include the module, the Exchange protocols are off until an administrator enables them. While they are disabled, the server behaves as if they did not exist.
- It stores nothing until it is used. Outlook and the other Exchange clients keep properties that no standard protocol has a place for: extended properties, reminder state, client settings. Stalwart stores them as metadata attached to the item they belong to, using the JMAP Object Metadata extension, and only writes them when an Exchange client connects and sets them. Accounts that are never opened by an Exchange client carry no Exchange data at all.
- Its data can be removed. Because the Exchange-specific properties live in that metadata and not in the messages, events and contacts themselves, deleting the metadata removes every trace of them while the items stay intact for IMAP, JMAP, CalDAV and CardDAV clients.
Migration from Exchange and Microsoft 365
Section titled “Migration from Exchange and Microsoft 365”
A drop-in replacement is only useful if the data can follow. Vandelay, our account import and export tool, migrates mailboxes from both sides of Microsoft’s offering:
- Exchange Server on premises, through the EWS importer, which reads mail, calendars and contacts.
- Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online), through the Microsoft Graph importer, which reads mail, calendars, contacts and OneDrive files. The EWS importer also works against Exchange Online, for as long as Microsoft keeps its EWS endpoint running.
Vandelay copies each account into Stalwart over JMAP, and the domain moves to Stalwart when its MX records and client settings change. The migration guide for hosted services walks through the whole process, from the first test account to the cutover. With the Exchange protocols enabled on Stalwart, Outlook and the other Exchange clients then connect through Autodiscover and find the migrated mail, calendars and contacts.
Other changes in 1.2.0
Section titled “Other changes in 1.2.0”
Exchange support is the headline, but 1.2.0 brings several other features, most of them developed alongside it because an Exchange replacement needs them:
- Mail rules. Server-side rules in the familiar “when a message matches these conditions, do this” form, managed in the WebUI, over JMAP or from Outlook. Conditions cover senders and recipients, subject and body, headers, size, attachments, importance, message type, mailing lists, spam score, date ranges and weekly schedules. Actions include moving and copying, marking as read or as junk, forwarding, replying with a template and rejecting. Rules are compiled into Sieve together with the vacation response. Each account also gets junk email lists: blocked senders, safe senders and safe recipients. See Mail rules.
- Read receipts. Message Disposition Notifications (RFC 8098), including the JMAP methods for sending and parsing them (RFC 9007).
- Working hours. Per-account working hours, managed in the WebUI, over JMAP or through CalDAV. Time outside working hours appears as unavailable in free/busy lookups, and a new setting lets users of the same organisation see each other’s free/busy time without sharing calendars explicitly. See Availability.
- Rooms and equipment. Resource accounts with a capacity, a location and delegates who manage the calendar, with invitations booked automatically or approved by hand. See Resources.
- Native FoundationDB client. A new asynchronous Rust client replaces Apple’s libfdb_c library. It needs no client library on the host and is now part of the standard build and Docker image. In our benchmarks it delivers between 4.5 and 6.9 times the throughput of the previous client on point reads, with 5 to 7 times lower median latency and about half the CPU.
The changelog lists every change and fix, along with the upgrade steps: existing servers need to add the new permissions to their default roles.
Stalwart CLI 2.0
Section titled “Stalwart CLI 2.0”
Last week we also released version 2.0.0 of stalwart-cli, and its biggest addition is an interactive console. Run stalwart-cli with no arguments in a terminal and it opens a full-screen interface that covers the same ground as the WebUI: browsing and editing accounts, domains and every other configuration object, watching the dashboard, following live traces and running actions. It is aimed at administrators who live in SSH sessions, or who work on hosts where opening a browser is impractical.
The console is built with Ratatui, the excellent Rust library for terminal user interfaces, and it is schema-driven like the rest of the CLI: its screens, forms and field help come from the schema that the server publishes, so it picks up new objects without being updated. The CLI also learned to sign in with the OAuth device flow and to remember the session, so a single approval in the browser is enough for both the console and every subsequent command.
FOSDEM 2027
Section titled “FOSDEM 2027”
Stalwart will be at FOSDEM 2027 in Brussels. We will have a Stalwart stand, and on Saturday, 30 January 2027, we will give a talk about moving from Microsoft Exchange to Stalwart in the Modern Email devroom. If you are planning a migration away from Exchange, or are curious about what it takes, come and talk to us. We will post the time and title of the talk once the schedule is published.
Until then, the Exchange documentation has everything needed to try it, and we would love to hear how your Outlook clients get on with Stalwart.

articles.title: US To Blacklist Asian AI Firm Megaspeed After Nvidia Scandal
articles.body:
US To Blacklist Asian AI Firm Megaspeed After Nvidia Scandal (bbc.com) 59
			
		 	
				The U.S. Commerce Department plans to blacklist Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed and its subsidiary Speedmatrix over suspicions that they helped Chinese companies obtain restricted Nvidia AI chips. The move follows allegations that a former Megaspeed executive had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while working as a Chinese intelligence asset, although Commerce officials say their investigation into the company began nearly two years ago. The BBC reports:  The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US. The company is mainly a developer of data centers, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang. [...] When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang. Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US. China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.title: New magical shows worth watching instead of Harry Potter
articles.body:
Since we wrote earlier this year about J.K. Rowling using her money to support groups and policies harming transgender people, she has accused the United Nations of promoting “sex denialism” and described trans rights activists as “elitists” whose work creates “a climate of fear and intimidation.” Also, her upcoming HBO Harry Potter series has not looked particularly good in any of the clips that have been released so far.
New magical shows worth watching instead of Harry Potter
Now’s a great time to get into some of this year’s best streaming fantasy series.
This take on Rowling’s novels appears to be a visually uninspired rehash of Warner Bros.’ film adaptations that’s designed for people who can’t free themselves from the shackles of nostalgia. But this year, there have been plenty of other new and returning shows that are filled with the kind of magic and mystery that gets fantasies going. And with the holiday season coming up, it’s the perfect time to give some of these less-problematic series a watch.
Percy Jackson and the Olympians
The second season of Disney’s adaptation of Rick Riordan’s fantasy series picks up at a time when all Percy Jackson (Walker Scobell) wants it to get back to Camp Half-Blood and reunite with his best friends Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri). But when Percy arrives at the camp, Annabeth acts like she wants nothing to do with him, and Grover has gone missing under mysterious circumstances. The peril Grover seems to be in prompts Percy to embark on an adventure to the Sea of Monsters to save him. It’s the kind of quest that turns demigods into legendary heroes, but it’s one that pushes Percy to his limits. Compared to last season, this chapter of Percy Jackson and the Olympians appears to be more epic in scale as it fleshes out its world of Greek gods and monsters. And now that the new season is airing, it’s a must-watch for fans of Riordan’s novels.
Coven Academy
When Briar Roberts (Malina Weissman) first arrives at Crescent Veil Academy in New Orleans, she assumes that the place is just a ramshackle school for delinquent teenagers. Briar thinks she’s been shipped off to Crescent Veil because of her anger issues and run-ins with the police. But headmistress Emma Graves (Tiffani Thiessen) and the other students quickly make it clear that they — like Briar — are powerful witches whose magic makes them targets for evil monsters. Coven Academy’s a pretty classic coming-of-age story that feels like a cross between American Horror Story: Coven and Degrassi: The Next Generation. It’s cheesy, but it’s an easy watch if you’re looking for something lighthearted on Disney Plus.
Witch Hat Atelier
Adapted from Kamome Shirahama’s manga series, Witch Hat Atelier tells the story of Coco (Anjali Kunapaneni) — a young girl who dreams of becoming a witch even though she doesn’t seem to have any innate mystical abilities. In the land of the Zozah Peninsula, only a select group of people are allowed by the Great Hall of Witches to practice any sort of magic. But when Coco accidentally casts a powerful spell by reading from a book, the witch Qifrey (Joshua A. Waters) takes her in as his latest apprentice. Witch Hat Atelier is one of the most gorgeous fantasy anime to hit Crunchyroll in 2026. Even if witchcraft isn’t really your thing, it’s a tremendous show that’s worth a watch.
VisionQuest
As a synthezoid powered by genuine artificial intelligence, Vision (Paul Bettany) prefers to think of himself as a man of logic and reason. The former Avenger understands he is a machine built by a team of engineers, but on some level, he also knows that the Scarlet Witch’s magic played a role in his becoming the newest version of himself. Even with that knowledge, Vision has a difficult time processing his feelings when he crosses paths with Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica), a Scottish orphan who seems to have a spiritual connection to the robotic hero. And to make things worse, Vision has to deal with his homicidal father, Ultron (James Spader), trying to make him relive traumatic memories. Following Agatha All Along, VisionQuest cements the WandaVision trilogy as one of the most riveting stories Marvel has produced to date. The series is brilliant on its own, and it portends some very promising things for the MCU’s future.
Bass X Machina
Set in an alternate, steampunk past where people are trying to settle the Wild West with the help of autonomous machines, Netflix’s Bass X Machina follows bounty hunter Bass Reeves (Brian Tyree Henry) as he finishes his last gig before retiring. Reeves is trying to leave the gunslinging life behind him in order to spend time with his family, but with money being tight, he can’t afford to give his robotic shooting arm a rest just yet. If Reeves had his way, he would just bag a couple of ordinary outlaws, collect their bounties, and be on his way. But fate has other plans, and Reeves winds up journeying into Choctaw Country on a mission to investigate a local man’s mysterious disappearance. Though Bass X Machina initially seems to be a straightforward steampunk anime, it takes a surprisingly magical turn that infuses its story with intrigue. And the show’s visuals are stunning — which isn’t a surprise given that it’s produced by Studio Mir.
Carrie
Mike Flanagan’s adaptation of Stephen King’s seminal novel for Amazon isn’t exactly fantasy, but it does present Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) as part of a group of women who have been historically persecuted for having talents that seem otherworldly. When Carrie comes across a book about women accused of being witches, she can’t help but see herself in their stories and she wonders if she, too, might be burned at the stake if people learn her secret. Though this spin on Carrie stays fairly faithful to the novel, Flanagan modernizes the story in order to tackle the realities of how kids bully one another in the age of social media. And while the show definitely takes some creative liberties that might confound King’s fans, it features one of the most terrifying (in a good way) depictions of Carrie’s fateful prom.
Small Prophets
Though Michael Sleep’s (Pearce Quigley) nosy neighbors know that he’s up to something strange in his shed, they have no idea that he’s experimenting with a recipe to grow prophetic homunculi in jars. According to a book of alchemy owned by Sleep’s father, Brian (Michael Palin), properly raised homunculi have the supernatural ability to accurately answer any question they’re asked. Sleep isn’t entirely convinced that what he’s doing will work, but he toils away in hopes that the humanoid creatures will be able to help him locate his long-lost girlfriend. As much as Small Prophets is a comedy, it’s also a touching drama about grief and the challenges of building new friendships as people enter the latter stages of their lives. Like many British series, Apple TV’s Small Prophets is a pretty quick watch, and it has already been renewed for a second season.
The Vampire Lestat
In its third season, AMC’s Interview With the Vampire gets a rebrand that mirrors the way Lestat de Lioncourt (Sam Reid) reinvents himself as the front man of a rock band. Lestat’s music career gives him a way to continue thumbing his nose at vampires’ laws about secrecy and to take his mind off his former lover, Louis de Pointe du Lac (Jacob Anderson). Try as they might, it’s hard for Lestat and Louis to stay away from one another, even though it strains their romantic entanglements with others. And the closer the two get to reconciling their relationship, the more innocent people around them get gravely hurt. Though this series has always been phenomenal, The Vampire Lestat reaches new emotional heights that make you feel how much these characters have evolved over time. And this season sets the stage for yet another surprising pivot into one of Anne Rice’s best stories.
American Horror Story: 13
Rather than committing to a completely new story the way previous chapters have, American Horror Story: 13 brings back a number of characters from past seasons. Almost every single cast member reprises multiple roles, and the show spins a wild tale that occasionally feels like a return to the series’ glory days — particularly when it’s focused on Supreme witches Cordelia Goode (Sarah Paulson) and her mother, Fiona (Jessica Lange). Though all of the witches can sense that a powerful evil is rising, they don’t know that Constance Langdon (also Lange) plays a pivotal role in the strange happenings across the world. Constance herself doesn’t fully understand what her new boss Mr. Nas (Paul Anthony Kelly and Fedor Steer) is trying to accomplish, but she follows his orders because she has faith that their desires are aligned. American Horror Story: 13 is at its best when it leans hard into camp and lets its ensemble cut loose as they move through the season’s ridiculous twists. And while it’s nowhere near as good as American Horror Story: Coven, it’s just great to see Lange hamming it up on the small screen again.
The Witch Farm
Inspired by real-world events, the BBC’s four-part series The Witch Farm tells the story of an English family who move to a remote house in the Welsh wilderness for a fresh start. At first, Liz (Gabrielle Creevy), her husband Bill (Michael Socha), and their son Jonathan (Lewin Lloyd) love their rustic new home, but it isn’t long before they begin to suspect that a malevolent presence is lurking in the shadows. While Liz and Bill don’t believe in ghosts, they can’t ignore the way people in their small town speak about their house as a place of evil. And as the couple learns more about the house’s history, they start to realize that they might have really wandered into a nightmare. The Witch Farm is only available to stream on BBC iPlayer, and it looks like a solid spooky treat for folks who love haunting horror.

articles.title: The search for a top dark matter candidate
articles.body:
The Search for a Top Dark Matter Candidate Was Losing Hope. Then Came a Potential Signal. Will It Be Enough to Energize the Struggling Field?
Physicists were growing weary with WIMPs, one proposed contender for the particles that make up dark matter. Despite their new cautious optimism, many challenges remain
Italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory is not a bad place to fret over the state of your career. The lab’s panoramic views of white-capped mountains and endless greenery are nearly inescapable. Physicists fuel their work with sharp espressos, rather than the watery coffee many Americans accept.
The lab also descends into the Gran Sasso mountain, forming one of the world’s largest underground research centers. Nestled beneath 4,600 feet of rock is an array of particle detectors. Thanks to the mountain’s thick skin, these instruments are shielded from cosmic rays, the high-energy particles produced by black holes, exploding stars and even our own sun. In the quiet depths of this laboratory, physicists hope to pick up on much more elusive particles—including dark matter.
For the past few decades, scientists have been hunting for dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up 85 percent of the matter in our universe. One primary target has been weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs—a hypothesized candidate for dark matter that passes through normal matter with barely a trace. Massive underground detectors like those at Gran Sasso are leading the search.
But no one has definitively found a WIMP, so no one is sure that they exist—and challenges to spotting them are building. As detectors get more sensitive, new background signals are beginning to cloud them, reducing the odds of catching WIMPs. Funding is growing more precarious, leaving many wondering how many years this endeavor has left.
When I visited the lab in May, the mood among some of these physicists was muted. “Of course, we were a bit more depressed,” reflects physicist Paolo Salomone, laughing. Despite his clear enthusiasm for the dark matter hunt, Salomone, a strikingly blue-eyed University of Chicago postdoctoral scholar, knew he was entering a field some might diagnose as terminal.
Then, in September, a pinprick of hope emerged. An American lab also searching for WIMPs released a preprint paper detailing a single—but intriguing—data point, rising above the expected background signals. Maybe, just maybe, it was dark matter.
Salomone was on vacation in Corsica when his phone started blowing up. Text notifications from physicist friends streamed in, asking him if he’d seen the news. “I was there on the beach trying to look at my phone, trying to zoom in on the plot,” he says. Watching the faraway excitement, he says, “I felt like I was missing out a lot.”
The finding was not a definite dark matter detection—one data point isn’t nearly enough to count as a discovery. Still, the result spawned headlines across the globe, a torrent of preprint papers and newfound hope for many physicists in search of WIMPs.
The question, now, is what’s next. Will this life raft be enough to overcome the field’s growing challenges? And will the few other detectors with similar sensitivity—most notably, one at Gran Sasso—be able to replicate the signal?
Nearly a century ago, Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky noticed a group of galaxies with some moving so quickly that they should have escaped the cluster’s gravity and flown apart. He theorized that some invisible material was gluing them together. Since then, scientists have accrued more evidence for this dark matter: stars speeding precipitously fast around a galaxy’s rim; unexpectedly strong gravitational lensing, in which distant light is bent by extreme gravity.
To explain it all, astrophysicists dreamed up WIMPs in the 1980s. As far as subatomic particles go, these would be relatively massive. In theory, they glide through space, on occasion lightly interacting with matter. Physicists have a pretty good sense of the density of dark matter scattered throughout our universe, but not much more about it. “It opens the possibility of having a lot of light particles or very few heavy particles,” says Salomone.
Directly detecting WIMPs, then, could clue us into the mass of individual dark matter particles and the number of them floating around, as well as how strongly these particles interact with normal matter. But finding them has been a challenge. Not only are physicists searching through a vast plain of possibilities, but they’re also looking for incredibly rare interactions that require extreme care in detection.
The smallest impurities can anger a detector. To illustrate the point, Marcello Messina, the technical coordinator for Gran Sasso’s XENONnT experiment, brought up the humble banana. While we don’t tend to think of a banana as radioactive, the fruits are rich in potassium, leading to a tiny shower of particle decays. “A banana can completely destroy our data table,” he said.
Messina was my guide for the day at Gran Sasso, driving me six miles through one of Italy’s longest tunnels and into the mossy interior of the mountain. He led me through the lab’s sterile halls, ending up at his even more sterile detector.
Messina’s XENONnT experiment is a hulking cylinder that holds a chamber of nearly 9.5 tons of xenon—mostly liquid—inside. The hope is that when a WIMP flies into the detector, it jostles one of the large and stable xenon atoms, which would in turn shoot out electrons and a light ray, alerting sensors to the strange particle’s presence.
XENONnT, which has been collecting data for around six years, is the strapping great-grandchild of the team’s original 2006 prototype. “XENON, for almost all its life, provided the most sensitive results,” Messina told me. “It was definitely leading the field.” Today, a few more rivals—like the American detector—have emerged.
We walked past another device that looked like a gigantic red Lego: a new detector Salomone is helping to build, DarkSide-20k, which will use a chamber of around 55 tons of argon instead of xenon. This enormous detector will reach a similar sensitivity to XENONnT and is set to begin collecting data in 2028.
Despite their materials’ purity, physicists expect some level of background fuzz—mainly radioactive decay products—and predict what that will look like. Sometimes, though, this “background” can behave in unexpected ways, so physicists must have a high bar for what anomalies in their data to take seriously.
Messina showed me a kind of memento mori for physicists: the latest generation of the DAMA experiment, which made a claim of dark matter detection that has been dismissed by most of the community.
In 1997, DAMA, which is made up of sodium iodide crystals, detected a signal that varied yearly, swooping in every summer—just as dark matter was expected to do. But while the team has continued to stand by their results, other experiments later ruled this out.
After DAMA’s false alarm, “I think people are just very cautious now,” says Ina Sarcevic, a physicist at the University of Arizona.
Despite the fear of more detector-cried-wolf scenarios, many physicists quickly pulled together theories to explain September’s announcement of a possible detection, Sarcevic says. The signal came out of South Dakota’s LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, which is currently the world’s largest WIMP detector.
Physicist Richard Gaitskell, LZ’s spokesperson, has been searching for dark matter for nearly 40 years, starting with a detector “barely bigger than the top of my thumb,” he says. LZ, on the other hand, is a nine-foot-tall cylinder containing around 11 tons of xenon, packed within a 20-foot-tall outer structure.
To take advantage of LZ’s whopping size and sensitivity, Gaitskell says, the team “decided to really aggressively push” beyond the usual search parameters.
The longstanding assumption in these experiments has been that WIMPs swoop in at relatively low energies and bounce off the xenon like billiard balls. - Others are hoping to create WIMPs. According to some theories, WIMPs might be produced by energetic collisions between normal particles.
Even if interest in WIMP detection is revitalized, technological challenges remain. One specter still haunting the field is a fog of neutrinos that’s threatening to descend on the instruments.
With increased sensitivity, the detectors are starting to pick up the constant swarm of neutrinos. These tiny particles don’t interact much with matter—trillions move through your body every second—but they can clutter data taken by detectors that are precise enough to notice them. As this neutrino fog wafts in, potential WIMP signals could get lost in the haze. XENONnT reported its first glimpses of the fog in 2024.
This isn’t a huge problem for the detectors yet, and not everyone agrees it will be soon. But once neutrinos start meaningfully gumming up the signal, scientists don’t know what they’ll do.
Ronald Walsworth’s group is experimenting with a workaround: tracing the direction of incoming particles. WIMPs are expected to flood in like a “headwind” against the solar system’s path through the galaxy, he says. On the other hand, a lot of neutrinos emanate from the direction of the sun, produced by the churn of fusion.
A sea of liquid xenon functions “like an antenna,” says Daniel Ang, a quantum scientist in Walsworth’s group. The flash of light only clues scientists into a particle’s collision—not the direction it rode in. So to trace a signal’s source, physicists might have to take a whole new approach.
Walsworth decided to try this by using a more glamorous substance: diamonds. From his previous work, he knew that when particles cut through diamond crystals, they leave behind a finely detailed track—so their incoming direction is clear. “That’s the grandiose idea we had,” says Walsworth, a quantum physicist at the University of Maryland.
But the team has only tested their blinged-out detector on a small scale, and getting the funds to go bigger will be a challenge—especially given the “sagging of enthusiasm” for WIMPs, Walsworth says.
Once Salomone, the postdoc, got back from vacation, his excitement about LZ’s signal was slightly tempered by his boss, he says. “He was, of course, more skeptical and less enthusiastic than me.”
But even among Salomone’s liquid argon detector community, scientists are paying serious attention to the result. His collaboration has a regular meeting, which only one or two dozen people usually show up to. But at a recent one, some 100 people attended. Even people who never participated were interjecting with ideas, he says.
Salomone’s workdays are much like before, continuing to help build the DarkSide-20k detector, placing orders for special screws and popping over to the café for an espresso. But he feels a renewed excitement about the theory behind his daily tasks.
“You’re still doing what you were doing before but with a different mind-set,” he says. “Spending more time trying to read papers, spending more time trying to be even a better physicist, so that’s what I’m really happy about.”

articles.title: Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a U.S. blacklist
articles.body:
Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the alleged Chinese espionage scandal involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S. Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor reported Monday.
The company will be added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, the outlet writes. This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.”
Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.”
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China. The company has denied wrongdoing.
TechCrunch reached out to the Commerce Department for comment on the reporting and will update this story if it responds.
After lobbying from President Trump, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday after a short period in which he was ousted by the company’s board over the scandal involving Huang.

articles.title: How to Make a Lovable City
articles.body:
Everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.
The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.
Sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.
Sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.
Anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte showed, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.
Create enclosed spaces
The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.
While the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.
The picture above shows the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.
Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.
London’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.
An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.
Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above shows Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.
Squares should not be too large
If a square is too large, it loses its sense of enclosure, and its buildings look strangely diminished by their surroundings. Sitte provided a rule of thumb in sizing squares: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it. The pictures above show two examples of over-large squares: the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest. Both feel demoralizingly vast, with the monumental buildings they are meant to showcase (Madrid Cathedral, and Budapest’s Hall of Art) dwindling to visual insignificance on the horizon, so that they resemble doll’s houses. In both squares, the buildings are so miniaturized that they no longer seem like enclosing walls, leaving the visitor exposed in a huge open space. This problem could be solved by making the buildings much taller, but although the square would then feel enclosed, the buildings would have become terrifyingly huge, as if meant for giants rather than human beings (the courtyard of Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris is an example of this pitfall in the wild).
Some of the world’s most famous squares are, in fact, far too large. St Peter’s Square in the Vatican, seen above, was designed by the famous artist Bernini, and it does indeed look impressive in drone footage. For human visitors, however, it is an exhausting place, overwhelming without being impressive. The Basilica looks small and stubby, exactly the opposite of the desired effect. On a summer’s day, the vast, unshaded space becomes relentlessly inhospitable, and visitors huddle under the colonnades for shelter.
By contrast, the small square in front of the Pantheon in Rome exemplifies the features Sitte prized. It is impossible to fully capture its feeling of enclosure in a two-dimensional photograph, but some sense of the intimacy of the space is apparent in the pictures above, which show how this magnifies the Pantheon. The Pantheon is a smaller building than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, but it is much bigger relative to the square. This allows it to retain its dignity, despite the fact that the level of the street has risen by 1.3 meters since Antiquity, swallowing the steps that originally led up to the entrance.
Symmetry is overrated
At the time Sitte was writing, many planners believed that harmonious spaces should have regular, symmetrical plans, an idea which remains influential today. In English we even use the confusing word ‘square’ for any enclosed public spaces, whatever their shape.
Sitte rejected this, believing that symmetrical spaces do not necessarily feel harmonious at ground level, and that asymmetry is not generally disharmonious at all. The pictures above show the perfectly symmetrical Place Vendôme in Paris. Seen from a satellite, it is visually striking and certainly neater than an irregular space. Its chamfered plan supposedly inspired the design of Chanel’s No 5 perfume bottle. Pedestrians, however, generally do not stand at the exact point at which the objective balance of the buildings is reflected in their field of vision: the various points and angles from which they do experience it may even make it feel quite awkward.
Above is the Piazza delle Erbe, a market square in Verona. This ‘square’ has an odd shape, an elongated and slightly wonky pentagon. Nobody is likely to model perfume bottles on it. But at human level, this does not matter as pedestrians can never take in all five sides at once, and so its irregular form is barely even visible. For the most part, the irregularities are ‘seen only on paper’, and to the extent they are visible, they are not experienced as imperfections. Sitte argued that they in fact serve to subtly arouse visual interest, and also create happy recesses that can host resting places, statues, or other public art.
Move monuments to the edges
If you were putting an ornament in your living room, you would be very unlikely to stand it in the middle of the carpet. It would get in the way, break up the space, and might well look lost and isolated. Nor would you place it in front of one of the room’s main features, like the fireplace. It would block the view of the fireplace, and the fireplace would be a disagreeably busy backdrop. Almost certainly, you would put it against the wall, preferably a relatively neutral wall to create a calm background.
Sitte thought the same considerations applied to the placing of sculptures, fountains, and other monuments in outdoor spaces. Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares, where they would block natural routes, break up the space, and look isolated and diminished. Nor should they be placed on axes with key buildings, where they block the view of the architecture. Instead they should line the sides, where they can stand out against relatively neutral backgrounds.

Buildings need context

Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.
Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘New Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.
Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.

Samuel Hughes is an editor at Works in Progress.

articles.title: How to Make a Lovable City
articles.body:
Everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.
The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.
Sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.
Sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.
Anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte showed, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.
Create enclosed spaces
The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.
While the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.
The picture above shows the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.
Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.
London’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.
An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.
Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above shows Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.
Squares should not be too large
If a square is too large, it loses its sense of enclosure, and its buildings look strangely diminished by their surroundings. Sitte provided a rule of thumb in sizing squares: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it. The pictures above show two examples of over-large squares: the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest. Both feel demoralizingly vast, with the monumental buildings they are meant to showcase (Madrid Cathedral, and Budapest’s Hall of Art) dwindling to visual insignificance on the horizon, so that they resemble doll’s houses. In both squares, the buildings are so miniaturized that they no longer seem like enclosing walls, leaving the visitor exposed in a huge open space. This problem could be solved by making the buildings much taller, but although the square would then feel enclosed, the buildings would have become terrifyingly huge, as if meant for giants rather than human beings (the courtyard of Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris is an example of this pitfall in the wild).

On a summer’s day, the vast, unshaded space becomes relentlessly inhospitable, and visitors huddle under the colonnades for shelter.
By contrast, the small square in front of the Pantheon in Rome exemplifies the features Sitte prized. It is impossible to fully capture its feeling of enclosure in a two-dimensional photograph, but some sense of the intimacy of the space is apparent in the pictures above, which show how this magnifies the Pantheon. The Pantheon is a smaller building than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, but it is much bigger relative to the square. This allows it to retain its dignity, despite the fact that the level of the street has risen by 1.3 meters since Antiquity, swallowing the steps that originally led up to the entrance.
Symmetry is overrated
At the time Sitte was writing, many planners believed that harmonious spaces should have regular, symmetrical plans, an idea which remains influential today. In English we even use the confusing word ‘square’ for any enclosed public spaces, whatever their shape.

Its chamfered plan supposedly inspired the design of Chanel’s No 5 perfume bottle. articles.title: Jevons Paradox in AI: Cheaper Tokens Won't Pay for Capex
articles.body:
Cheaper AI Tokens Won't Pay for $560 Billion of Capex
Updated 24 November 2026
Contents
Key takeaways
- Token volume and token prices are moving at roughly the same speed, so cheaper inference on its own does not grow AI revenue.
- The price of a fixed level of capability collapses each year, while the cost of running frontier models rises; the revenue sits at the frontier.
- Closing the gap between capex and revenue needs money that today pays for labor, and outcome pricing is how vendors are reaching for it.
- The capex and cash flow figures from March have grown worse: five hyperscalers spent $560 billion in the first three quarters of 2026.
In March I wrote that the hyperscalers’ answer to collapsing inference prices is Jevons: cheaper tokens create so much demand that total spending grows anyway.
On volume, they look right. Google processed 9.7 trillion tokens a month in May 2024. In May 2026 it was 3.2 quadrillion, 330 times as many. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle spent $230 billion on capex in the third quarter of 2026 alone, almost four times what they spent two years earlier.
But tokens aren’t dollars. Revenue is price times volume, and the price is falling too. So my question is: does demand for tokens grow faster than the price of a token collapses?
The arithmetic
If the price of a token falls 10x and volume grows 10x, revenue is flat. Revenue only grows when volume grows faster than the price falls.
Google’s first-party model APIs went from 7 billion tokens a minute in Q3 2025 to nearly 32 billion in Q3 2026, up 4.6x. Google’s tokens across all products grew 6.7x between the I/O keynotes of 2025 and 2026. OpenRouter went from 0.5 trillion to 128 trillion tokens a week in 20 months, about 27x a year. On the price side, MIT researchers find that the price of reaching a fixed benchmark score falls 5 to 10x a year, and Epoch AI finds that cost per task at fixed performance falls about 13x a year.
Volume and price move at about the same speed. That proves nothing by itself, because Google’s tokens aren’t sold at fixed-capability prices (like the ones Epoch measures). But it lines up with what Mert Demirer, Andrey Fradkin, Nadav Tadelis and Sida Peng found when they used OpenRouter and Azure data to estimate short-run price elasticities “just above one” and concluded that this leaves “limited scope for Jevons-Paradox effects.” At an elasticity of one, a 10x price cut buys 10x the tokens for the same money.
That matches how a lot of buyers behave. Say a bank’s head of operations has $2 million approved for AI contract review, and then the vendor cuts its token prices tenfold. The bank can now review ten times as many contracts, which is great. The budget still says $2 million. To spend more, the head of operations would have to walk into the CFO’s office and argue that the product got cheaper and so deserves a bigger budget, and I wouldn’t want to make that case. So the bank spends the same $2 million. The vendor can say, truthfully, that token volume grew tenfold.
But I guess there’s also a counterargument. Cheaper tokens change what people build. When inference is nearly free, developers design agents that call a model hundreds of times per task, and a recent theory paper argues this can make demand rise faster than prices fall. That may happen.
Two price curves
“The price of a token” hides two curves that move in opposite directions. (1) The price of a fixed level of capability is falling. GPT-4-level answers cost a small fraction of what they did in 2023, and the decline continues. (2) The cost of using the best model available is rising. The same MIT paper finds that the cost of running frontier models on benchmarks rises 3 to 18x a year, because each generation is larger and reasons for longer.
A concrete case: to run the Artificial Analysis benchmark suite, Claude Opus 5.5 at maximum effort used 218 million output tokens, almost three times the median model, at about $10 per task. At low effort the same model used about a tenth of the tokens.
Spending probably follows the frontier curve (at least up until now). In enterprises, open-weight models now handle 19% of tokens but get 4% of spend, while frontier labs take 69% of deployment dollars. Cheap tokens and expensive tokens are close to two separate markets (the cheap one grows fast in volume and barely registers in revenue).
The volume is real
I don’t want to wave the demand away. Google’s token count is the clearest public series we have, and it’s steep.
Agents account for much of it. A paper by Bai, Brynjolfsson, Pentland and co-authors finds that agentic coding tasks use about 1,000 times more tokens than chat about the same code. Anthropic reported in 2025 that multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chat. OpenRouter dates February 6, 2026 as the last day humans used more tokens on its platform than agents did.
Where the money has to come from
If cheaper tokens alone don’t grow revenue, the money has to come from somewhere else. Bain estimates AI needs $2 trillion of annual revenue by 2030 to fund the compute being built, and that it will still be $800 billion short even if companies reinvest every dollar AI saves them in sales, marketing, support and R&D.
You can already see vendors reaching for that money in their pricing. Intercom charges $0.99 for each customer case its Fin agent resolves, a price set against the cost of a support agent’s time, whatever the tokens cost. Salesforce has changed its Agentforce pricing three times since 2024. The direction is clear. Vendors want to be paid per outcome, and an outcome is priced against a (human) wage.
Workers aged 22 to 25 in the jobs most exposed to AI saw a 13% relative drop in employment compared with less exposed peers. US employers cited AI in about 121,000 announced job cuts in the first ten months of 2026, about a fifth of all announced cuts.
Receipts
Spending grew faster than I expected when I wrote in March. Back then the five companies guided to $660 to $690 billion for 2026. Their SEC filings show $560 billion of cash capex in the first three quarters, with $230 billion in Q3 alone. That excludes finance leases, so the full figure is higher.
The cash flow squeeze I described has arrived. Oracle spent 174% of its operating cash flow on capex in its fiscal 2026 and Amazon 94% in 2025. Microsoft is at 63%, Meta at 60% and Alphabet at 56%, all well above where they were a few years ago.
Who keeps the money
So far the clearest winner is the company selling the equipment. Nvidia reported $116 billion of revenue at a 75% gross margin in its latest quarter, and its revenue has grown in step with hyperscaler capex for three years.
The model labs sit lower. Press reports put OpenAI’s gross margin at 33 to 39%, depending on the quarter. Anthropic’s S-1 shows about an 85% gross margin, but it books training compute under R&D, so the figure only measures the cost of serving existing models. Even so, it suggests the cost of serving tokens may be falling faster than their price.
Markets have priced the split. Since ChatGPT launched, the semiconductor index has roughly tripled while software stocks and the S&P 500 are both up about 70%. Chips have also fallen 41% from their June peak, so the market is less sure than it was in the summer.

articles.title: Jevons Paradox in AI: Cheaper Tokens Won't Pay for Capex
articles.body:
Cheaper AI Tokens Won't Pay for $560 Billion of Capex
Updated 24 November 2026
Contents
Key takeaways
- Token volume and token prices are moving at roughly the same speed, so cheaper inference on its own does not grow AI revenue.
- The price of a fixed level of capability collapses each year, while the cost of running frontier models rises; the revenue sits at the frontier.
- Closing the gap between capex and revenue needs money that today pays for labor, and outcome pricing is how vendors are reaching for it.
- The capex and cash flow figures from March have grown worse: five hyperscalers spent $560 billion in the first three quarters of 2026.
In March I wrote that the hyperscalers’ answer to collapsing inference prices is Jevons: cheaper tokens create so much demand that total spending grows anyway.
On volume, they look right. Google processed 9.7 trillion tokens a month in May 2024. In May 2026 it was 3.2 quadrillion, 330 times as many. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle spent $230 billion on capex in the third quarter of 2026 alone, almost four times what they spent two years earlier.
But tokens aren’t dollars. Revenue is price times volume, and the price is falling too. So my question is: does demand for tokens grow faster than the price of a token collapses?
The arithmetic
If the price of a token falls 10x and volume grows 10x, revenue is flat. Revenue only grows when volume grows faster than the price falls.
Google’s first-party model APIs went from 7 billion tokens a minute in Q3 2025 to nearly 32 billion in Q3 2026, up 4.6x. Google’s tokens across all products grew 6.7x between the I/O keynotes of 2025 and 2026. OpenRouter went from 0.5 trillion to 128 trillion tokens a week in 20 months, about 27x a year. On the price side, MIT researchers find that the price of reaching a fixed benchmark score falls 5 to 10x a year, and Epoch AI finds that cost per task at fixed performance falls about 13x a year.
Volume and price move at about the same speed. That proves nothing by itself, because Google’s tokens aren’t sold at fixed-capability prices (like the ones Epoch measures). But it lines up with what Mert Demirer, Andrey Fradkin, Nadav Tadelis and Sida Peng found when they used OpenRouter and Azure data to estimate short-run price elasticities “just above one” and concluded that this leaves “limited scope for Jevons-Paradox effects.” At an elasticity of one, a 10x price cut buys 10x the tokens for the same money.
That matches how a lot of buyers behave. Say a bank’s head of operations has $2 million approved for AI contract review, and then the vendor cuts its token prices tenfold. The bank can now review ten times as many contracts, which is great. The budget still says $2 million. To spend more, the head of operations would have to walk into the CFO’s office and argue that the product got cheaper and so deserves a bigger budget, and I wouldn’t want to make that case. So the bank spends the same $2 million. The vendor can say, truthfully, that token volume grew tenfold.
But I guess there’s also a counterargument. Cheaper tokens change what people build. When inference is nearly free, developers design agents that call a model hundreds of times per task, and a recent theory paper argues this can make demand rise faster than prices fall. That may happen.
Two price curves
“The price of a token” hides two curves that move in opposite directions. (1) The price of a fixed level of capability is falling. GPT-4-level answers cost a small fraction of what they did in 2023, and the decline continues. (2) The cost of using the best model available is rising. The same MIT paper finds that the cost of running frontier models on benchmarks rises 3 to 18x a year, because each generation is larger and reasons for longer.
A concrete case: to run the Artificial Analysis benchmark suite, Claude Opus 5.5 at maximum effort used 218 million output tokens, almost three times the median model, at about $10 per task. At low effort the same model used about a tenth of the tokens.
Spending probably follows the frontier curve (at least up until now). In enterprises, open-weight models now handle 19% of tokens but get 4% of spend, while frontier labs take 69% of deployment dollars. Cheap tokens and expensive tokens are close to two separate markets (the cheap one grows fast in volume and barely registers in revenue).
The volume is real
I don’t want to wave the demand away. Google’s token count is the clearest public series we have, and it’s steep.
Agents account for much of it. A paper by Bai, Brynjolfsson, Pentland and co-authors finds that agentic coding tasks use about 1,000 times more tokens than chat about the same code. Anthropic reported in 2025 that multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than chat. OpenRouter dates February 6, 2026 as the last day humans used more tokens on its platform than agents did.
Where the money has to come from
If cheaper tokens alone don’t grow revenue, the money has to come from somewhere else. Bain estimates AI needs $2 trillion of annual revenue by 2030 to fund the compute being built, and that it will still be $800 billion short even if companies reinvest every dollar AI saves them in sales, marketing, support and R&D.
You can already see vendors reaching for that money in their pricing. Intercom charges $0.99 for each customer case its Fin agent resolves, a price set against the cost of a support agent’s time, whatever the tokens cost. Salesforce has changed its Agentforce pricing three times since 2024. The direction is clear. Vendors want to be paid per outcome, and an outcome is priced against a (human) wage.
Workers aged 22 to 25 in the jobs most exposed to AI saw a 13% relative drop in employment compared with less exposed peers. US employers cited AI in about 121,000 announced job cuts in the first ten months of 2026, about a fifth of all announced cuts.
Receipts
Spending grew faster than I expected when I wrote in March. Back then the five companies guided to $660 to $690 billion for 2026. Their SEC filings show $560 billion of cash capex in the first three quarters, with $230 billion in Q3 alone. That excludes finance leases, so the full figure is higher.
The cash flow squeeze I described has arrived. Oracle spent 174% of its operating cash flow on capex in its fiscal 2026 and Amazon 94% in 2025. Microsoft is at 63%, Meta at 60% and Alphabet at 56%, all well above where they were a few years ago.
Who keeps the money
So far the clearest winner is the company selling the equipment. Nvidia reported $116 billion of revenue at a 75% gross margin in its latest quarter, and its revenue has grown in step with hyperscaler capex for three years.
The model labs sit lower. Press reports put OpenAI’s gross margin at 33 to 39%, depending on the quarter. Anthropic’s S-1 shows about an 85% gross margin, but it books training compute under R&D, so the figure only measures the cost of serving existing models. Even so, it suggests the cost of serving tokens may be falling faster than their price.
Markets have priced the split. Since ChatGPT launched, the semiconductor index has roughly tripled while software stocks and the S&P 500 are both up about 70%. Chips have also fallen 41% from their June peak, so the market is less sure than it was in the summer.

articles.title: Top MIT Physicist: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About 'Taking over the World'
articles.body:
Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist
Apparently they discuss overthrowing the US government after a few drinks.
by Clare Hymer
24 November 2026
Employees at US artificial intelligence company Anthropic openly talk about “overthrowing the US government” and “taking over the world”, a world-renowned physicist has claimed.
In an interview with Novara Media, Max Tegmark, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said: “When I talk to people who work for Anthropic, after they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world.”
“They tend to not use words like ‘coup’ and ‘overthrow the US government’. They instead use the code phrase ‘alignment without control’,” he said.
‘Alignment without control’ is the idea that AI should be kept in check by being instilled with certain values – likely those shared by Anthropic, Tegmark said – rather than being directly controlled by humans.
“We get the sort of future that Alan Turing predicted, where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine-god running Earth, and then the rest of us just have to hope that somehow it’s gonna be nice.”
Turing, widely regarded as the founder of computer science, famously warned in 1951 that once machines started thinking, we should expect them to take control.
Tegmark said the comments from Anthropic staff should alarm anyone who cares about democracy. “These companies really don’t seem to like it [democracy]. They have lobbied really hard to even prevent any meaningful government oversight of them,” he said.
He added: “Here in the US, OpenAI and Anthropic are less regulated than a sandwich shop.”
Novara Media has approached Anthropic for comment.
Tegmark’s disclosure comes as protests against AI are ramping up across the world.
As Anthropic started trading on the stock market at a staggering $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters gathered at both the Nasdaq exchange in New York and the firm’s San Francisco headquarters demanding an AI development slowdown.
On Saturday, over 1,000 people marched against “AI extinction” in London in what campaigners said was “the biggest AI safety march in history”.
Clare Hymer is head of articles at Novara Media.
