FAQ
Declare is a programming language for user interfaces — a domain-specific language, the way SQL is a domain-specific language for querying data. You describe an interface as a tree of views with attributes; any attribute can be a live expression, and when the things it reads change, everything that depends on it updates. All real logic is ordinary TypeScript. Programs compile in the browser or ahead of time, and one program renders to the DOM, directly to pixels on a canvas, or as a native Mac app.
Because most of what makes UI code hard isn't your application — it's the plumbing. In Declare there is no render lifecycle to manage, no state synchronization to orchestrate, no CSS cascade to fight, no build pipeline to configure. An application is a readable tree of declarations: the flagship calendar — four views, continuous zoom, drag-to-reschedule — is about 600 lines of code you can read end to end. Given the same brief, an agent's Declare app came out at half the code of its React app. And Declare is built for the era when much code is written by machines: the language is small enough to hand a model in its entirety, and strict enough to verify what comes back.
Declare is at its best where an interface has to be designed, not just assembled: custom, fluid experiences of the kind you find in the best native apps — calendars, editors, dashboards, product sites — where views become one another and motion carries meaning. Everyday apps come with it: forms, lists, settings screens and admin tools are what the library's controls are for, and content-heavy apps work well (Markdown rendering is built in). Everything on this site is a Declare program: the homepage, the documentation, the calendar, the desktop.
An AI can produce a standard-looking app easily, and in Declare it can produce one verifiably. A custom experience is a set of decisions — how it should look, how it should move, what should happen when — and those come from human judgment and direction. What Declare changes is how directly those decisions can be expressed in code: layout, motion, states and theming are the language itself, so what you meant stays legible in the code, and the AI that writes it, the compiler that checks it and the colleague who reads it later are all looking at the same design.
Yes, with effort. Windows that drag, resize and layer; minimizing into live thumbnails; a magnifying dock; menus that follow focus; other programs running inside windows — in a mainstream web stack each of those is usually its own library or its own project, and keeping them coherent (focus, stacking, hit-testing, animation that can be interrupted) is where the effort goes. In Declare they are the language and its library, and the desktop is one program of 2,011 lines of code. That is why it makes a good acid test for any UI toolkit.
Time and change live in the language instead of being bolted on:
- Constraints — any attribute can be a { } expression; the compiler works out what it depends on, and it stays current. No re-render ceremony, no manual subscriptions.
- Animation as declaration — springs and animators are attributes; states are named bundles of overrides you can be in or not in.
- Layout as an attribute — how a view arranges its children is a value you set, not a system you fight. And layouts are written in Declare too: a class with one method, place(), so a layout of your own is no harder to make than to use.
- Controls you can write — the library's buttons, sliders and menus are ordinary Declare classes. Extend Control and yours takes clicks, taps, focus and keys exactly as theirs do, so there is no cliff between using a component and building one.
- Drawing and effects in the same tree — draw(), clipping to any shape, filters and backdrop blur are attributes of a view, alongside its layout and motion, not a separate canvas or effects layer.
- Performance from the model — because the compiler knows every dependency in advance, the reactive core runs as a small C kernel: WebAssembly in the browser, native on the Mac. That cut update time 42–53% on every platform measured, and made a window drag’s updates five or more times faster.
- Data binding — UI replicates over data with a cursor (datapath), and two-way binding connects editable fields to the data they edit.
- One input model — pointer and keyboard events are routed identically on every renderer, with a built-in keyboard focus system.
It's a language, not a framework inside JavaScript. In React and its relatives, the UI is a function you re-run — the framework diffs the output and patches the page, and you manage the machinery (hooks, memoization, effects) that keeps re-running affordable. In Declare, the UI is a standing structure: values flow through it when things change, and nothing re-renders because nothing was ever a render. There is also no HTML/CSS/JS trinity — structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language. Its nearest relatives are declarative-tree systems like SwiftUI and QML, but Declare is web-native, compiled, renderer-independent, and uses TypeScript — not a new scripting dialect — for logic.
The compiler parses the declarations, statically extracts every constraint's dependencies, type-checks every { } body as real TypeScript against every class's typed API, resolves the components you use (the standard library auto-includes by name), and emits a self-contained program. The benefits: errors surface before the program runs, with messages that name the fix; reactivity is derived by the compiler, not guessed at runtime, so behavior is predictable and analyzable by tools; production output is small; and programs are data — the same compiler powers the documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing. The compiler itself runs anywhere — in Node, or in the browser.
The [ ] structure is Declare; everything inside { } — expressions, event handlers, methods — is ordinary TypeScript, type-checked with full knowledge of every class's attributes. There is no new expression language to learn. The declarative layer contributes structure and reactivity; TypeScript contributes logic — and everything you (or your model) already know about it carries over.
A reusable view is a class: class PriceTag [ … ]. Its attributes are its public interface, and it reports back through events it declares. Composition is just nesting: your classes are used exactly like built-ins, including replication over data.
No — and that's a feature. Styling is part of the language: paint attributes on views (fill, cornerRadius, stroke, shadow, text styles), theme records that reskin an entire subtree from one place, and named style bundles a subtree can switch between at runtime. Your CSS knowledge transfers — colors (named or hex), font stacks, shadows all read the same — but there is no cascade, no specificity, no selector debugging. This is also what makes renderer independence possible: the canvas renderer couldn't consult a stylesheet the browser owns.
Side by side, yes; interleaved, no. A Declare app embeds in any page — including a React page. And inside a Declare program, the DOMIsland view hosts foreign content — a video player, a code editor, a React widget — in a box the Declare tree sizes and positions. What you can't do is put a React component inside the Declare tree as if it were a Declare view, or vice versa. The boundary is always an island, which is what keeps both sides comprehensible.
No router is needed: the URL is just an attribute. Declare location on your app and it follows the address bar. Setting it navigates, Back restores it, and a deep link is simply its starting value; the rest of the app derives from it like any other value. In the docs on this site, #guide/14-data opens that chapter directly. Deep-linked pages are crawlable too.
At build time, the compiler runs the app headlessly and bakes its content into the page as plain HTML: real headings, paragraphs and links. Crawlers and AI readers get that; people get the live app. No server needed: this site runs on GitHub Pages.
Because the compiler runs in the page, the page can edit and re-run itself: every sample on this site is live-editable — change the source and the app re-renders as you type. It restores view-source culture: "View and edit source" on any app here opens the viewer — a highlighted reader, the verbatim source, and a live-edit tab (?viewer=edit on the program's URL). And it means development needs no build step — the dev server and the browser use the same compiler with byte-identical output. For production you don't ship the compiler: the declarec build precompiles everything into a small artifact, no compiler aboard.
One program renders through managed DOM elements, directly to a single canvas, or in a native Mac host — same tree, same layout, same input handling, the three held to each other by a conformance suite (append ?render=canvas to any app URL to see it). The Mac host is a native macOS application, AppKit layers in place of DOM nodes, with the runtime's kernel linked in natively; you build it from the repository with one command (npm run build:mac). What this buys: the language owns its semantics — no DOM assumptions leak into your program; the canvas path suits environments where a DOM isn't available or isn't fast enough; and future renderers can be added without rewriting applications. Programs also run headlessly — no screen, no renderer at all — which is what powers static extraction and testing.
Concretely, measured from the deployed production artifacts:
- Wire size: the entire Declare calendar — application and runtime — ships at about 177 KB gzipped (the homepage reports the live figure, measured from the deployed production artifacts on every commit, which is why it can vary by a kilobyte).
- Source size: the tracker — a million issues, search as you type, editing in place with undo — is 1,508 lines: 983 of code and 251 of comments, and no dependencies. It ships at 194 KB gzipped before its data, which a DataSource fetches at run time.
- Responsiveness: when you drag an event, the constraint graph updates exactly what changed and paints — there is no virtual-DOM pass between your gesture and the pixels. Animations ride compositor-native paths (CSS transforms and painted properties on the DOM renderer; direct paint on canvas), so they run at the display's full rate — 120 fps on a ProMotion screen.
- Finding what's slow: the profiler (declare-profile, or the Inspector while you use the app) says which of your rules ran, how often and for how long, what each class cost to build, what drawings cost the GPU, and how long each frame took to reach the screen — in the program's own terms, its classes, attributes and source lines, never the runtime's internals. It runs in the browser or the Mac host.
- Startup: precompiled production builds start immediately. The live-compile pages (the editable samples) pay a one-time compiler download on a cold visit; warm visits start in around a tenth of a second. The one honest trade: a framework with no in-browser compiler wins the very first cold load — Declare's production path closes that gap by precompiling.
Live numbers are on the homepage, measured from the deployed artifacts themselves.
When machines write the code, the properties that matter change. Familiarity matters less; verifiability matters more. Declare's bet: give the model a small, closed, regular language, and give the toolchain the strictness to catch what the model gets wrong. Every compile type-checks every expression — a hallucinated attribute or misused API is an error with a message that names the fix, so the model's write-check-revise loop converges fast. And because an entire application is a few hundred lines of declarations, what the model produced can actually be audited — by a person or by another model. The calendar on this site reports its own number: zero lines written by hand.
Human-designed and directed, built with AI. The calendar was built by describing what was wanted and letting an LLM write the Declare — every line — with the compiler in the loop: each attempt was compiled and type-checked, the diagnostics steered the next revision, and the running app was the judge. The person's work was product design work — deciding what the calendar should be, reviewing behavior, and pushing back — not typing code. That's the workflow the language is designed around: the human owns intent, the model owns the text, and the toolchain keeps the text honest.
Two ways. First, the language is small enough that its entire definition fits in a model's context window — one file, docs/declare.md, about 21,000 tokens: a small fraction of a modern context window. A model doesn't need to have trained on a language it can hold the complete spec of while writing; recent research (cited in the essay on this site) shows models write never-before-seen languages competently from a spec in context. Second, most of what an LLM writes in a Declare program is covered by billions of lines of training data — the logic is ordinary TypeScript. Only the small declarative shell is new, and it's regular enough to learn from the spec. For agent workflows, the repository ships the same knowledge as an installable agent skill (skill/ — auto-discovered by Claude Code, usable as plain instructions by any coding agent).
verify command compiles, type-checks, boots the program in a real browser at laptop and phone sizes, and drives it with real input, so an agent can prove its output works before handing it back.
Starting cold from the repository, agents have built complete apps and passed hidden acceptance checks they never saw:

They are single runs, not yet a benchmark, and every one is published in full, the agent's own account included.
It's tested, not assumed. Agents are given a brief for a complete app and the repository, cold, and build it start to finish. Hidden acceptance checks they never see then drive the result through its controls' accessible names, both as delivered and at the first build that ran. The same brief goes to React, and to more than one vendor's model, and each run is published in full with the agent's own account of it, word for word. Failures feed back into the language, the diagnostics, and the documentation — several language changes exist specifically because evals showed models tripping. The documentation is written to double as training material: plain declarative prose, and every code fence in the teaching docs is compiled by the test suite, so nothing a model reads is stale or wrong. The result is a feedback loop — spec, diagnostics, evals — rather than a hope.
Declare is a from-the-ground-up modern successor to OpenLaszlo, the open-source rich-internet-application platform first released in 2002. OpenLaszlo had the core ideas remarkably early: interfaces declared as trees, attributes connected by live constraints, declarative data binding, compiled applications running in the browser — a decade before today's declarative frameworks. Declare keeps those convictions — the declarative tree, constraint-based reactivity, a real compiler — while rebuilding everything else for the modern era: a clean keyword-free syntax, TypeScript for logic, DOM and canvas renderers, in-browser compilation, and a design shaped from day one for the LLM era.
David Temkin, who co-founded Laszlo Systems and led the team behind OpenLaszlo. He writes about what led from one to the other at the end of the "Why Declare" essay.

Declare · runtime architecture
A Declare front end is one self-contained artifact — small enough to hold in your head, strict enough for a machine to verify, rich enough for an ambitious application. This is what Declare’s runtime does to make that true.
Declare asks you to believe something unusual about an application’s front end: that it is complete. Everything the interface does — where each box goes, how a paragraph wraps, what a click landed on, how a view becomes the next one — is written in the one program, as relationships rather than steps, so a machine can verify it and a person can read it. That puts a demand on what runs underneath: if the browser decided the layout, or the DOM routed the click, the program would not be complete. So the runtime makes those decisions itself, once, and hands the browser what it does best.

The compiler is where completeness is enforced. It parses the brackets into a tree, resolves every name to an explicit path, extracts what every { } body reads, and type-checks each body as TypeScript against the real interface of every class — so an attribute that doesn’t exist, or a relationship that reads something it can’t, is an error before anything runs. What it emits is not code that builds a UI but a description of one: the tree, a graph of which value reads which, and, for every body that is plain arithmetic, bytecode for a small stack machine. One line of the homepage’s bouncing-ball demo, compiled:
You wrote
to = { on ? lane.width - ball.width : 0 }
Resolved
to = { this.root.on ? parent.parent.parent.lane.width - parent.parent.ball.width : 0 }
Read-paths
0 this.root.on
1 parent.parent.parent.lane.width
2 parent.parent.ball.width
Kernel code
"=EL0 L1 L2 - K0 ?" — load 0, 1, 2 · subtract · push 0 · select
Because the program is data, it can be questioned as data. The Inspector on any page here — ⌥⌘D — reads this same graph: click a value and it shows the body that produced it, everything that body read, and their live values. The same completeness is what lets an AI’s work be checked: the compiler, the Inspector and verify all read one description of the whole interface, not a guess pieced together from files.

Which view is under the pointer, and whether this was a click or the start of a drag, are the runtime’s answers, not the browser’s — one implementation under a finger or a pointer, on every renderer. And the settle itself runs in a kernel: one C file of about 1,400 lines that holds the graph’s tables and evaluates the compiled arithmetic, shipped as WebAssembly (10 KB gzipped) and linked natively on the Mac. 03
A Spring is an attribute with a target; each frame it writes its next value, and that write is a settle like any other. Nothing about animation is special-cased, so a new target mid-flight is simply the next write: the spring retargets from wherever it is, and everything that read it follows. Interruptibility isn’t a feature of an animation system; it is what a reactive graph does when you write to it.
Every box is decided before the host hears of it — by arithmetic over attributes, by a layout (a class with one method, place()), or by the content’s own size. Text is the one place the host contributes a number, the width of a glyph; wrapping and height are the runtime’s, so a paragraph breaks into the same lines on every renderer. Because the runtime placed every box, it also answers the inverse question — what is under this point — and that one answer decides hover, press, and where a drag lands.
04
Because the compiler hands over the whole graph up front, the runtime doesn’t have to discover anything as it runs. Its reactive core (the graph, the settle, and the arithmetic of layout, springs and visibility) is a small C kernel: WebAssembly in the browser, linked natively on the Mac. Bodies that are plain arithmetic arrive as bytecode the kernel evaluates itself, without returning to JavaScript.
Moving the core there cut update time by 42–53% on every platform measured (Chrome, iOS Safari and the Mac host), and a window drag’s by 81–93%. The rules evaluated didn’t change; each one simply costs less.
05
Everything above happens on one side of a single interface, Surface — 71 methods such as setX, setFill and setText that the runtime calls and a backend implements. The DOM backend keeps an element per view and hands the browser what it does best: real text, the page’s own scroll, links, native fields. The canvas backend draws the tree directly to pixels. The Mac host is a Swift application with no web engine in it, applying each settle to Core Animation layers. Drawing (draw(d)) records rather than paints, so each host replays the same recording its own way.
Below, the calendar’s build drawn to scale by gzipped bytes: switch hosts and one block is exchanged while everything else holds still. Beneath it, the same desktop program on each host.

A web page embeds a Declare app with one attribute on a sized element; inside a Declare program, a DOMIsland gives a video player, an editor or a React widget a box of its own, and an AppIsland hosts another Declare program — this article is one, inside the homepage. In a browser a Declare app is a web page, not an imitation of one: text selects and finds, fields are native, scroll is the page’s own, links ⌘-click and Back tells the truth, and a crawler reads a static extraction from a plain host. articles.title: The AI conversation we're not having
articles.body:
8 Things Two Years in AI Taught Me That Nobody Posts About
AI is threatening everyone. That is the feeling, anyway.
I’ve been working in AI for about two years now. Most recently that’s been at Arcade.dev, helping teams get their agents into real production use. I’m still figuring a lot of it out, like everyone else.
Over these two years, the same questions keep finding me. A friend over dinner wondering if their job is safe. A customer trying to figure out where to even start. Someone new to tech, and someone with decades in it, both quietly asking what actually matters now. I don’t have all the answers, but I’ve collected a few honest ones. Here are eight things I keep coming back to.
1. Do not doubt the skills you already have
What you have built over years is legitimately useful, even if the ground is shifting under it. Your old skill may be transcending into something else. Figure out what that something else is. But do not start by throwing away what you have.
Compounding still works in skills. It is still working.
And you’re not the only one feeling it. Everyone is adjusting to how fast things are moving. Everyone is going through a disruption in their career and their life, and everyone is working hard to get through it. It is not the whole world ending. It is the whole world changing at the same time.
And if you’re just starting out, you have something the rest of us don’t: no baggage. You haven’t spent ten years learning “the right way” to do things that may not matter anymore. Use that. Try the weird idea. Just remember that a fresh idea only counts once you’ve built it.
2. Meet people in person
The digital world is getting weird. More automation, more bots, more noise. So do more of what AI cannot do.
Have food with people. No robot is going to split a pizza with you and ask how your family is doing. Go meet a friend in person and say hello. It opens up perspectives you will never get inside the tech bubble.
That is how I got my job. I met people in person. A LinkedIn profile is a vastly different thing from the person standing in front of you.
3. Your originality is the leverage
There is exactly one person in the world who is like you. No one can replace that. So go after it, big time. I know it is hard. Go after it anyway.
If someone comes after your originality, they have already lost, because they are admitting they do not have their own.
There is always some value you can add in a given situation, regardless of money, title, or anything else. And that value compounds too. Test it.
4. Build something real. Not something fancy.
I see a lot of people talk about agents. Some are even trying to build critical agent infrastructure, and they have not built two agents for themselves.
Building agents is hard. It is not running a prompt. There is deployment, scaling, quality, evals, design, model choice, prompting, cost. Do not underestimate any of it.
If you’re new, this is your edge. Almost every hiring manager will ask the same question: what have you built? So build. Contribute to an open source project. Ship a rough idea. Put something out there that works, even if it’s ugly.
But don’t confuse building with building a lot. Just because you can build something doesn’t mean you should. Knowing what not to build is a skill too. Building what people actually need is vastly different from building something fancy that no one is going to use.
Talk is cheap. Build the right thing.
5. Adoption is slow. Wait for it.
Almost none of this technology has reached real scale yet, outside a few model companies. True adoption happens slowly, because habits are hard to break.
At the end of the day, humans are the consumers of this technology. They pay from their own pockets. They are the economy. AI will take time to make money, and that is exactly where you can make money too, if you are in the industry.
So do not conclude too early. Do not get frustrated. Do not build FOMO. I am not an AI optimist. I am skeptical of many things. But doomsday is not coming either. There will be a place for you to keep adding value.
Wait for habits to break. Wait for people to embrace agents. Wait for people to understand the patterns.
6. Join problem solvers, and ask hard questions
In any industry, look for the people solving a really hard problem. Find that group and join it.
Do not be fooled by a fancy marketing site. In my experience, the people who do not know the depth of building a product end up with the fanciest marketing. The people building great products often do not have time to polish theirs.
So when a company vibes well with you, question it deeply. Who are their customers? How will they sustain long term, financially? How do they make money? If the market crashes, do they have enough funding secured to survive it? What are their case studies? Do they have a sales team?
Ask those questions before you join, not after.
7. Study the past
History repeats itself. That is why we call something a pattern: because it is one.
You have all this fancy AI. Use some of it to study the past. What happened when the internet arrived? When cars were invented? When world wars reshaped everything? You will find clues about what is going to happen to you. Use them as a wedge to reinvent yourself. There is no other choice.
8. Nobody retires from what they love
Billionaires will tell you money will become invalid and nobody will need to work. Regardless of all that, your hard work, your focus, and your perspective are not going away. Your energy is always going to be there. You have to put it on something.
Do not fall for the retire-at-forty trap. Nobody actually retired. Some people made more money. Some stopped working for a company. But nobody ever retired from their passion. Nobody retired from doing the thing they love.
Working for yourself, building something meaningful, that is not going away.
Do something meaningful.
So, who are you going to meet next week? And what agent are you going to build tomorrow?

articles.title: Trump Halts Army's Plans to Detonate Bomb-Making Chemicals In Iowa
articles.body:
Trump Halts Army's Plans to Detonate Bomb-Making Chemicals In Iowa (arstechnica.com) 84
			
		 	
				President Trump has ordered the military to halt plans to detonate nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. "Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January," reports Ars Technica. From the report:  The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).
Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.
Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice's request to put a hold on the Army's permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to Buy Zscaler In $44 Billion Deal
articles.body:
CrowdStrike to Buy Zscaler In $44 Billion Deal 25
			
		 	
				CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire network security provider Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal. "The deal marks CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition to date and is among the largest in the sector as businesses consolidate and ramp up defenses to fend off AI-powered attacks," reports CNBC. The acquisition is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028. From the report:  "With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said in a statement. "We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen."
CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open. Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge. Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion.
[...] Analysts view the Zscaler deal as a major AI security opportunity, allowing CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending and close a significant gap with Palo Alto. "The addition of ZS to CRWD's platform could bring more breadth in an era of vendor consolidation and, more importantly, network security to position the company more effectively for rising demand for AI Sovereignty," wrote analysts at JPMorgan.

articles.title: UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
articles.body:
The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.
The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post.
The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.
The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.
While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.
“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.
The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.
The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”
The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

articles.title: Six Artworks Under $1,000 We’d Love to Give (and Receive!) This Holiday
articles.body:
Six Artworks Under $1,000 We’d Love to Give (and Receive!) This Holiday
There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. These types of gifts are often the most unexpected, surprisingly personal, and typically, one of a kind.
Our partners at Joy Machine have generously curated a selection of artworks that fit this category. Priced under $1,000, the collection includes pieces by an international group of artists that longtime Colossal readers will surely recognize. From playful drawings in walnut ink to uncanny kitsch sculptures, these works are perfecting for gifting this holiday season, even (especially?) if that gift is to yourself.
Seattle-based artist Debra Broz applies her training in ceramic conservation to a practice that involves scouring flea markets and thrift shops for ceramic figurines, breaking their forms, and reassembling the figures as surreal hybrids.
Dutch artist Collin van der Sluijs is a master of several styles, with a background in graffiti and street art and a parallel interest in the delicate, impeccably detailed features of the natural world.
Collect “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” ($550)
With a deep love for the flora and fauna near her home in the Pacific Northwest, Stevie Shao creates folk art-inspired works through bold color palettes and arresting patterns.
Japanese artist Misato Sano is best known for her cheeky wooden carvings of poodles and pugs, which she translates to two-dimensions in this playful rendition that might just make us want to get up and get moving.
Collect “Let’s work out” ($150)
Through large-scale paintings and small woodcuts, Danym Kwon meditates on the mundane activities like folding laundry or strolling around the park that allow memories to emerge and be understood anew.
Collect “A Quiet Afternoon” ($350)
Layering acrylic paint with crisp edges that evoke paper collage, Rachel Hayden blends the patterns of a summertime picnic with the eerie colors and atmosphere of fall, perfect for the perpetually witchy pal.

articles.title: Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags
articles.body:
It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Meta’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.
While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.
The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.
In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.
The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.
Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

articles.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
articles.body:
Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

articles.title: The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
articles.body:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 23 Nov 2026]
Title:The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is never negative, yet PyTorch users have reported negative values for years, and the standard advice is to clamp them at zero. The sign is only the visible part of a silent failure. Many machine-learning applications compare nearby distributions, where conventional KL formulas lose accuracy. On 8.5 million inputs with certified references across 18 closed-form KL families and F.kl_div, we find widespread errors in values and gradients on CPU and GPU. Among scalar families in ordinary parameter ranges, over 85% of FP32 values have at least 1% relative error near KL 10^(-7) (FP16: 10^(-3)), and about 30% become negative at smaller divergences. More precision is not the cure: evaluated one precision higher, the same formulas still leave 7--51% of FP32 values significantly wrong for 22 of 23 configurations. Stable closed-form decompositions, compensated arithmetic, and analytic gradients remove over 97% of significant errors in the working format. Strict repairs eliminate significant errors on 7.2 million scored closed-form samples and correctly round all 567 million scored F.kl_div components. The errors affect parameter fitting, Bayesian decisions, identical-start distillation (up to 97% top-1 disagreement), KL-based layer rankings in a quantized LLM, and 19--59% of GPT-2 circuit edge scores. With the repaired code they all but vanish. Code and data: this https URL

articles.title: Levent Alpöge comments on his Riemann Hypothesis proof
articles.body:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

articles.title: Shirudo: OpenAI and Cisco's open-source runtime for shielding unpatched Linux
articles.body:
OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test(opens in a new window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.
We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.
Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.
Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.
Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.
OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:
- Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.
- Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.
- Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.
- Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.
The Shirudo technical walkthrough(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here(opens in a new window).
Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.
Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.
We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.
OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo(opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.
Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.
- Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart(opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.
- Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab(opens in a new window).
- Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar(opens in a new window).
We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub(opens in a new window), read the docs(opens in a new window), and let us know what you find(opens in a new window).

articles.title: Have You Been Attacked by an Owl?
articles.body:
Personally, I have not been attacked by an owl, but more than a few folks in nearby Brookline have. Possibly, per the associate director of field conservation at Zoo New England, by one of the weird owls.
Please also enjoy a chuckle at the article’s ambiguous headline:
Owls have attacked at least a dozen people in the Brookline area. I’m one of them.
Perhaps author Milena Fernsler is a victim of an owl attack. Alternately, perhaps Fernsler is an actual owl. Naturally, I prefer the latter explanation.
Previously in unprovoked avian assaults: I Was a Victim of Bird Strike

articles.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
articles.body:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
5 min read
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?
Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.
So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.
It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks
Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.
So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???
This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!
Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.
Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.
And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.
This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.
On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.
- And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎
